text: These questions follow the order of the appendix Embedded Databases: SQLite and DuckDB. Each of the four groups checks one or two sections of the appendix. The “Self-check” buttons in the appendix lead to these groups. Nothing you answer is recorded.

title: Embedded Databases Self-Checks
section: What an Embedded Database Is, and When to Use One
text:
What an Embedded Database Is, and When to Use One
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Which of these describe an embedded database? Select every one that applies.
Select all that apply.



Its database engine is a library that runs inside the program that opens it

Yes. When the program ends, so does the engine.



Its data is an ordinary file, or a directory of files, on the program’s own disk

Yes. Opening the database means opening the file.



There is no user to create and no password to enter

Yes. Thus, whoever can read the file can read the data.



It grants each user different privileges on its tables

Users and privileges are services of a server. An embedded database has neither.



It runs as a program of its own, installed and started before use

That is a server. An embedded database has nothing to install and start.



Check Show answer Reset



2. DataGrip, psql, and one of the book’s Kotlin programs all work with the book’s PostgreSQL database at the same time. What are they?



Clients, each connecting to the one server, signing in as a user, and sending it SQL

Yes. The server holds the data, enforces the constraints, and lets the clients work at once.



Three copies of the database engine, each running inside its own program

That is how an embedded database works. PostgreSQL’s engine is the server, a program of its own.



Three programs that open one shared database file directly

The data is held by the server, not opened as a file by each client.



Servers, of which the first to start holds the data

There is one server, always running. The tools and programs are its clients.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Embedded Databases Self-Checks
text:
SQLite
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. In a SQLite table that is not strict, quantity_on_hand is declared INTEGER. A program inserts the text 'forty' into it. What does SQLite do?



It refuses the insert, as PostgreSQL would

A declared type in SQLite is a preference, its type affinity, not a rule.



It stores the text, so the column holds text in one row and integers in others

Yes. typeof shows the mixture, and an analysis of the column later meets a value it did not expect.



It converts the word to the number 40

SQLite does not read words as numbers; it stores the text as given.



It stores NULL in place of the text

The column is NOT NULL, and SQLite keeps the text rather than discard it.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which statements about SQLite are true? Select every one that applies.
Select all that apply.



It has no date type; dates are stored as text in the ISO form, as numbers, or as both

Yes. SQLite’s date functions work on any of these.



Many connections may read at once, but a write locks the whole file briefly

Yes. One writer at a time suits one program, not a busy system.



A file holds one set of tables, and ATTACH opens a second file under a name where PostgreSQL would use a schema

Yes. SQLite has no schemas.



ALTER TABLE can add a foreign key to an existing table’s column

A foreign key cannot be added to an existing column; the table is rebuilt instead.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Which statements about foreign keys in SQLite are true? Select every one that applies.
Select all that apply.



A REFERENCES clause is parsed, but enforced only on a connection that runs PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON

Yes. SQLite does this for compatibility with old databases.



The setting lasts only as long as the connection that turned it on

Yes. It is not stored in the file.



The KSL’s SQLite connections turn it on

Yes. The KSL’s own connections enforce foreign keys, so the files they write do not meet this problem.



Once any connection turns it on, the setting is saved in the file for all later connections

The setting belongs to the connection, not to the file.



SQLite rejects a REFERENCES clause as a syntax error

SQLite accepts the clause. Whether it is enforced depends on the connection.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Embedded Databases Self-Checks
text:
DuckDB
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A table of simulation results has 20 columns, and a query averages 3 of them over every row. Why does a column store such as DuckDB suit this query better than a row store?



A column store keeps each row’s values together, so each row is read once

That describes a row store, such as PostgreSQL or SQLite.



A column store keeps each column’s values together, so the query reads only the 3 columns it needs

Yes. A column of like values also compresses well. A row store must pass over every column of every row it reads.



A column store does not need the rows to be stored at all

The rows are all stored; they are only arranged by column.



A column store finds and changes one row faster

Finding or changing one row touches one place in a row store. That is the row store’s strength.



Check Show answer Reset



2. True or False: in DuckDB, a column declared VARCHAR(10) refuses a value of twelve characters.



True

DuckDB accepts the length in a type and ignores it, so the longer value is stored without complaint.



False

Right. DuckDB enforces types, but not the length in one. A length rule that matters belongs in a CHECK constraint.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A file of replications is long, one row per replication and response. Which statement turns it wide, one column per response, with the columns found in the data rather than listed by hand?



A GROUP BY with one FILTER per response

That works in PostgreSQL, but the query lists each response’s column by hand.



DuckDB’s PIVOT, naming the column whose values become columns and the aggregate that fills each cell

Yes. PIVOT is DuckDB’s own statement; neither PostgreSQL nor the SQL standard has it.



DuckDB’s UNPIVOT

UNPIVOT goes the other way, from wide to long.



COPY to a Parquet file

COPY writes a result to a file; it does not reshape it.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Embedded Databases Self-Checks
section: Embedded Databases from Kotlin and the KSL, and Choosing a Database
text:
Embedded Databases from Kotlin and the KSL, and Choosing a Database
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. An analyst wants to summarize a KSL study’s results with DuckDB’s SQL, without adding DuckDB’s driver to any program. What is the usual route?



Open the KSL’s SQLite file directly in a Kotlin program with the URL jdbc:duckdb:

That URL needs DuckDB’s driver in the program’s build, which the KSL does not include.



Write the study’s views to CSV files with exportAllViewsAsCSV, and query those files in DuckDB

Yes. DuckDB reads a CSV file where a table’s name would stand, so no program of its own is needed.



Convert the study to PostgreSQL first, since DuckDB reads only from a server

DuckDB is embedded; it reads its own files, CSV files, and Parquet files.



Copy the rows into DuckDB by hand, since DuckDB cannot read CSV files

Querying CSV files directly is one of DuckDB’s strengths.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A Kotlin program opens jdbc:sqlite:stock.db. Where does the database engine run?



Inside the program: SQLite’s driver is the engine, and the URL names a file

Yes. The program needs only the driver’s library; there is no server to reach.



On a SQLite server that the program connects to

SQLite has no server. The URL names a file, not a host.



Inside DataGrip, which must be open while the program runs

DataGrip is a separate program. It can open the same file, but the program does not need it.



On the PostgreSQL server, which reads the SQLite file for the program

PostgreSQL plays no part. The driver reads and writes the file itself.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 2 Self-Checks
text: These questions follow the order of Chapter 2. Each of the first six groups checks one or two sections of the chapter, and the last group reviews the whole chapter. The “Self-check” buttons in the chapter lead to these groups. Nothing you answer is recorded.

title: Chapter 2 Self-Checks
text:
Tables, Rows, and Domains
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A designer stores each part’s dimensions in one text column, as values such as 24 x 18 x 10 (length, width, and depth in inches). Planners regularly ask which parts fit on a shelf 20 inches deep. Is the dimensions value atomic?



Yes, because each cell holds one string

Holding one string is not the test. “Fayetteville, AR” is one string too.



No, because a query needs the depth on its own, and the text gives the database no way to pick it out or check it

Yes. The test is a question about use: does any query, rule, or sort need part of the value on its own, in a way its domain does not supply? Here one does, so the three measures belong in separate columns.



Yes, because the value is short

Length does not settle it. A two-character state code is atomic and a long description may be too, depending on how each is used.



No, because it contains spaces

“Fort Smith” contains a space and is atomic. How a value looks does not settle the question.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which of these changes alters the customer table’s schema rather than its state?



Adding a column for each customer’s sales region

Yes. The schema is the table’s name, columns, and domains, and it changes when the database is redesigned.



Adding a ninth customer

A new row changes the rows the table holds now, which is its state.



Changing a customer’s city after it moves

Changing a value in a row changes the state.



Removing a customer that has no orders

Removing a row changes the state. The table can still hold exactly what it could hold before.



Check Show answer Reset

The schema is what the database can hold, and the state is what it holds now.




3. A designer gives an order table the columns product1, product2, and product3, one product number in each. What is wrong with this design?



Nothing; each cell holds one atomic value

Each cell does hold one value, but the three columns hold the same attribute, told apart only by position.



The three columns are a repeating group; an order with a fourth product needs a new column, and a search for one product must look in all three

Yes. The relational model forbids repeating groups and records such facts as rows of a table of their own, one row per product on the order.



The columns break the third property, since their names are too similar

The three names are different, so the third property holds. The trouble is what the columns hold, not what they are called.



Only the order of the columns is wrong; product1 should come last

The order of the columns carries no meaning. Reordering them changes nothing about the design.



Check Show answer Reset



4. A script adds rows to a table with INSERT statements that list values but do not name the columns. Later the table is rebuilt with the same columns declared in another order. What happens when the script runs again?



Nothing changes, since the columns of a relation have no order

That is the model. A SQL table keeps the order in which its columns were declared, and such a statement depends on it.



Its values go into the wrong columns, or the statement is refused

Yes. A statement that adds a row without naming its columns matches values to columns by position. A statement that adds a row should always name its columns.



PostgreSQL matches each value to the column with the same data type

The database does not guess. It matches values to columns by position when no columns are named.



The rows are added in a different order, but correctly

The statement adds the same rows as before. The trouble is which column receives which value.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 2 Self-Checks
text:
Keys
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. customer_number is a candidate key because HG Industries assigns each customer one number and never reuses it. Suppose the company began giving a closed customer’s number to a new customer. What follows?



customer_number stops being a key, and every report that assumed it was one would silently merge two customers’ histories

Yes. A candidate key is a fact about the business, so it holds only as long as the business’s rule does.



customer_pk stops being a key as well

customer_pk is generated by the database. How the business numbers its customers does not affect it.



Nothing, as long as the tables are not redesigned

The key rests on the business’s promise. When the promise changes, the key goes with it, whatever the tables say.



customer_number becomes a surrogate key

A surrogate key is a value the database generates, meaning nothing outside it. A customer number is business data either way.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Is the pair (customer_number, city) a candidate key of the customer table?



Yes, because no two customers share both values

That makes the pair a superkey. A candidate key must also be minimal.



No, because customer_number alone already identifies a customer, so the pair is a superkey but not a smallest one

Yes. A column can be removed from the pair without losing the property, so the pair breaks the second condition.



No, because a candidate key may have only one column

A key of several columns, a composite key, is a candidate key when no smaller set of its columns would do.



Yes, because adding a column to a key makes it safer

An extra column makes the set larger, not safer. It is still a superkey, but not a candidate key.



Check Show answer Reset



3. The stock_level table has the alternate key (warehouse_fk, product_fk). A clerk receives 50 more units of a product that a warehouse already stocks and tries to record them by adding a new stock_level row for that warehouse and product. What happens, and what should the clerk do?



The row is added, and the two rows together give the warehouse’s stock

The alternate key forbids two rows with the same warehouse and product, so the database never holds the second row.



The database refuses the row, since the warehouse already has a stock level for the product; the clerk should change that row’s quantity on hand instead

Yes. The key says that a warehouse holds at most one stock level for each product. Neither column alone is a key: a warehouse stocks many products, and a product is stocked in more than one warehouse.



The row is refused, because a foreign key column cannot be part of a key

Both columns are foreign keys, and together they are a key. A column may play both roles.



The row is added, since stock_level_pk gives it a new primary key value

A new surrogate key does not excuse a row from the alternate key. The database enforces every candidate key.



Check Show answer Reset



4. At stage D2, customer 1 appears three times in the customer_fk column of customer_order, and customer 8 does not appear at all. What does that pattern show? Select every statement it supports.
Select all that apply.



A customer may place many orders

Yes. Each of customer 1’s orders holds the same customer_fk.



A customer may be recorded with no orders

Yes. Nothing requires a customer to be referred to by any order.



customer_fk cannot be a foreign key, since its values repeat

A foreign key’s values may repeat. It is the key it refers to, customer_pk, whose values may not.



Customer 8’s row breaks referential integrity

The rule concerns the values of a foreign key. A customer that no order refers to breaks nothing.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 2 Self-Checks
text:
Integrity Rules
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A designer declares a foreign key’s response to deleting the row it refers to as SET DEFAULT. What must be true for a deletion to succeed under that response?



The column’s default must be NULL

A response that leaves the rows referring to nothing is SET NULL, a different response.



The column’s default value must itself match a row that exists in the table referred to

Yes. The rows that referred to the deleted row are given the default, and referential integrity still applies to it: a default that matches no row would leave them pointing at nothing.



Nothing; a default is never checked against the other table

The new value is a foreign key value like any other, and the rule applies to it.



The row being deleted must not be referred to by any row

A row that nothing refers to is deleted without any response at all. The response matters only for rows that are referred to.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A query lists each order beside the name of the customer who placed it, by matching customer_fk to customer_pk. Can an order’s customer_fk hold a value that matches no customer?



No; every value of a foreign key that is not NULL has a matching row in the table it refers to, and a query can rely on that

Yes. A foreign key is a promise the database keeps on every change, so the query never has to check for orphans itself.



Yes, whenever a customer has been removed since its orders were placed

Whatever response the designer declared, the database never leaves an order pointing at a customer that does not exist.



Yes, because the database checks foreign keys only when a query reads them

The database checks a foreign key when a row is added or changed, before the change is kept.



It depends on how the query is written

How a query is written cannot change the rows a table holds.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 2 Self-Checks
text:
Writing Down a Schema
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The complete relational schema of customer_order includes the line check: requested_ship_date >= order_date. What does it say?



A customer cannot ask for an order to ship before the order was placed, and the database refuses a row that would break the rule

Yes. A CHECK constraint narrows the domain of a column, here by comparing it with another column of the same row.



Every order must have a requested ship date

Whether a column may be NULL is said on its own column line, and requested_ship_date may be NULL.



Every order ships on or after the date it was placed

The check compares two columns of the order itself. Shipments and their dates are recorded in another table.



It is a note for readers that the database does not enforce

A CHECK constraint is part of the schema, and the database enforces it on every change.



Check Show answer Reset



2. The foreign key lines of the distribution schema sort its tables into groups. Which of its tables refer to no other table of the distribution schema? Select every one that does not.
Select all that apply.



customer

Yes. It has no foreign key.



warehouse

Yes. It has no foreign key.



product

Yes. Its one foreign key refers to production.manufactured_part, a table of another schema.



customer_order

An order refers to the customer who placed it.



stock_level

A stock level refers to a warehouse and to a product.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A bill of materials line has the columns assembly_fk and component_fk. What do the book’s naming rules tell you about them?



They are primary keys, one for each kind of part

A primary key column ends in _pk. A table has one primary key, and these columns end in _fk.



Both are foreign keys, each named for the role that the referenced row plays rather than for the table it refers to

Yes. A line names an assembly and one of its components, both parts, so naming each column after its table would not say which is which.



They refer to two tables named assembly and component

A foreign key is usually named for the table it refers to, but these are named for roles, since the rows they refer to are all parts.



The names alone settle every key, so the relational schema need not list them

The relational schema states the keys anyway: a key of several columns, an alternate key, and a database named by someone else’s rules all need saying.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 2 Self-Checks
section: The Catalog and the Tools That Read It
text:
The Catalog and the Tools That Read It
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A query names the column order_no, but the column of customer_order is named order_number. When does PostgreSQL find the mistake?



After it has read every row, when none has an order_no

The DBMS never gets that far. It checks every table and column a query names first.



Before it reads a single row, by looking the column up in the catalog

Yes. The DBMS reads the catalog more than anyone, and it refuses a query that names a column the table does not have.



Only when the result is shown, as an empty column

A query that names a missing column produces no result at all, empty or otherwise.



Never; it returns order_number, the nearest name

The database does not guess at names. It refuses the query and says which column does not exist.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which of these changes alter the catalog? Select every one that does.
Select all that apply.



Creating a table of machine maintenance records

Yes. Creating a table adds rows to the catalog, which describes the table and its columns.



Adding a column for each customer’s sales region

Yes. A new column is a change to the schema, and the catalog holds the schema.



Adding a ninth customer

A new row changes the state of the customer table, not its description.



Changing a warehouse’s quantity on hand of a product

Changing a value changes the state. The catalog changes only when the database is redesigned.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Why does the database tree of DataGrip or DBeaver have the same outline for any PostgreSQL database you connect to, even one you have never seen?



Because every database uses the schemas distribution, production, and quality

Those are HG Industries’ schemas. Another database has schemas of its own, and the tree shows them just the same.



Because the tool draws the tree from the database’s own catalog, which every relational database holds

Yes. A relational database is self-describing, so you can always ask it what it holds. psql’s \d command reads the same catalog.



Because the tool stores a copy of each database’s schema when it is installed

The tool reads the schema from the database each time it connects. It brings no copy with it.



Because the tree shows only the tables, which all databases share

The tree shows each database’s own schemas, tables, columns, keys, and constraints.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 2 Self-Checks
text:
Other Ways to Organize Data
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Which statement separates the relational model from the hierarchical and network databases that came before it?



Relational databases store data on disk, and the older ones kept it in memory

Where the data is kept is not the difference the chapter draws.



A relational database connects records by matching values, while the older ones connected them by stored links that a program followed

Yes. Because tables connect by values, any question can be asked in a query; in the older databases, an unplanned question meant a new program to walk the links.



The older databases could not represent a bill of materials

A bill of materials is a tree, which suited a hierarchical database well.



Relational databases are no longer used where the older ones once ran

The relational model replaced them for most uses, but IMS still runs in some banks and manufacturers.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A document database stores order SO-5001 as one JSON document, with the order’s lines nested inside it. What does a program gain from that arrangement?



A program that needs the whole order reads one document, without a join

Yes. A document database suits data that is written and read whole, such as an order or a test record.



The document must follow a structure declared for every order

Each document describes itself, and no catalog is needed to read it.



The order’s lines are kept in a table of their own, referred to by key

The lines are nested inside the order’s document, as a list.



Every field of the document must hold text

A field may hold a number, a list, or another document.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 2 Self-Checks
text:
Review of the Whole Chapter
Read the chapter summary

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Why does a SQL table need a key to keep the property that no two of its rows are identical?



Because a key sorts the rows, and identical rows would sort together

A key identifies rows. It has nothing to do with sorting them.



Because SQL does not require a table to be a true set, so a table with no key can hold two identical rows, which a relation never can

Yes. Every table in the book’s database has a key, and the database rejects any row that would repeat a key value.



Because without a key PostgreSQL refuses to create the table

PostgreSQL will create a table with no key. That is why the key must be declared.



Because identical rows are allowed only in query results

A query result may repeat a row, but so may a table with no key. The key is what prevents it in the table.



Check Show answer Reset



2. What was the appeal of an object database, which stores a program’s objects directly?



It connects records by matching values, as a relational database does

An object database connects objects by references, as the objects of a running program are connected.



The program’s classes and the database’s structure are the same thing, so nothing is translated between them

Yes. Object databases never displaced relational ones; relational systems took on some of their features, and libraries now do the translation.



It needs no description of its data, since every record names its own fields

That describes a document database, whose documents describe themselves.



It replaced relational databases in engineering design

It found uses there, but it never displaced relational databases.



Check Show answer Reset



3. You are handed a connection to an unfamiliar database and asked which customers received a given product. What should you do before writing a query? Select every step the chapter recommends.
Select all that apply.



Ask a tool for the schema diagram, or read the relational schema

Yes. Reading the map takes a few minutes and saves hours of guessing.



Find the tables that describe the things the request names, and trace a path of foreign keys between them

Yes. That path is the reasoning behind a join, and it shows which tables the query needs.



Guess the column names and let the refused queries correct you

The catalog already holds every name. Ask for it instead of guessing.



Copy the tables into a spreadsheet to look at them

The database describes itself, and the tools read that description directly.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 9 Self-Checks
text: These questions follow the order of Chapter 9. Each of the first four groups checks one section of the chapter, and the last group reviews the whole chapter. The “Self-check” buttons in the chapter lead to these groups. Nothing you answer is recorded.

title: Chapter 9 Self-Checks
text:
Views
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The view order_report joins orders, customers, order lines, and products. After it is created, one product’s description is changed with an UPDATE of product. What does the next query of the view show for that product’s lines?



The new description, on every line of the product

Yes. A view stores no rows. Each query that uses it runs the view’s query against the tables as they are at that moment, so the one changed row shows everywhere.



The old description, until the view is created again

That would be true of a stored copy. A view is a named query, not a copy of its result.



The old description on old orders and the new one on later orders

The view holds no history; every line reads the one current row of product.



An error, since a table under a view cannot be changed

The tables behind a view are changed as usual. The view simply reads them as they are.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which of these views does PostgreSQL make updatable automatically? Select every one.
Select all that apply.



A view of customer that keeps the rows WHERE state = 'OK'

Yes. It selects from a single table, and each of its rows comes from one row of customer.



A view of product that shows only product_number and description

Yes. Choosing some of a single table’s columns keeps each view row tied to one table row.



A view of customer that shows only the first ten customers, with LIMIT 10

LIMIT is among the clauses that keep PostgreSQL from making a view updatable automatically.



A view of stock_level that shows SUM(quantity_on_hand) for each product

A row of an aggregate comes from many rows, so the database could not tell which row a change should reach.



A view of customer that shows DISTINCT state

DISTINCT merges rows, so a view row no longer comes from one table row.



Check Show answer Reset



3. The view oklahoma_customer shows the customers WHERE state = 'OK' and was created WITH CHECK OPTION. What does the clause do?



It checks each customer’s state against a list of valid states

The clause knows nothing of valid states. It compares a row with the view’s own condition.



It refuses a change made through the view that would produce a row the view could not show, such as a customer in Arkansas

Yes. Without it, a clerk could add through the view a row that the view itself would never show.



It makes the view store its rows, so they can be checked

A view with the clause still stores no rows. A view that stores its result is a materialized view.



It lets a view over a join be updated

The clause does not make a view updatable. It limits the changes allowed through a view that already is.



Check Show answer Reset



4. True or False: because a view is defined in advance, a query of the view runs much faster than the same query written out with the view’s joins.



True

A view stores no rows, so its query still runs every time. Storing the result for speed is what a materialized view does, at the price of being current only when refreshed.



False

Correct. PostgreSQL merges the view’s query into the query that uses it, so the two cost about the same. A materialized view trades currency for speed and is brought up to date only by REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 9 Self-Checks
text:
Transactions and the ACID Properties
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. In PostgreSQL, a foreign key with NO ACTION is declared DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED. Inside one transaction, a statement leaves a row that refers to nothing, and a later statement repairs the reference before COMMIT. What happens?



The first statement is refused, since a foreign key is checked as each statement runs

That is how a key that is not deferred behaves. A deferred key waits.



The transaction commits, since the key’s check waits until COMMIT and finds every reference in place then

Yes. Deferring the check lets a transaction pass through an inconsistent state on its way to a consistent one.



COMMIT is refused, since the transaction once held a row that referred to nothing

The deferred check looks at the rows as they are at COMMIT, not at the states the transaction passed through.



The transaction commits only if the key’s action is RESTRICT

A RESTRICT check is never deferred. It is the NO ACTION key that can wait until COMMIT.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A transaction runs these steps in PostgreSQL:
BEGIN;
UPDATE stock_level ... ;   -- succeeds
SAVEPOINT before_carts;
UPDATE stock_level ... ;   -- refused
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_carts;
COMMIT;
What is committed?



The first UPDATE only

Yes. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work after the savepoint, here the refused statement, and the first update stays in the transaction.



Nothing, since a statement in the transaction failed

The savepoint marks a point to return to, and rolling back to it keeps the work done before it.



Both updates

The second update was refused, and it made no change to keep.



Nothing, since ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT ends the transaction

It ends nothing. Only COMMIT or ROLLBACK ends the transaction.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Against which events does durability protect a transaction whose COMMIT has returned? Select every one.
Select all that apply.



The database server crashes a minute later

Yes. PostgreSQL wrote the change to its write-ahead log before reporting the commit, and replays the log after a crash.



The machine loses power a minute later

Yes. A crash of the machine is recovered from the log in the same way.



The transaction was a mistaken DELETE

Durability keeps committed changes, mistaken ones included. Recovering the deleted rows takes a backup.



The disk that holds the database fails

The log is on a disk too. A failed disk or a lost machine calls for a backup kept elsewhere.



Check Show answer Reset



4. True or False: in DataGrip or DBeaver with the console in auto-commit, a DELETE typed by mistake can be undone with ROLLBACK, provided no other statement has run since.



True

In auto-commit, each statement runs in its own transaction and is committed at once, so there is nothing left to roll back.



False

Correct. The DELETE is permanent the moment it runs. To experiment safely, type BEGIN first and end with ROLLBACK.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 9 Self-Checks
text:
Concurrency and Isolation Levels
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Two clerks, each in a transaction, insert a customer with the same customer number, a UNIQUE column. Clerk A’s insert runs first, and A has not yet committed. What happens to clerk B’s insert in PostgreSQL?



It fails at once as a duplicate

A’s row is not committed and may yet be rolled back, so the database cannot yet say whether B’s row is a duplicate.



It waits until A’s transaction ends, then fails if A committed and goes ahead if A rolled back

Yes. Two inserts of the same value of a UNIQUE column wait for each other, as two changes of the same row do.



It succeeds at once, since B cannot see A’s uncommitted row

B cannot read A’s row, but the constraint must still account for it, so B waits.



Both succeed, and the duplicate is removed at the next COMMIT

A UNIQUE constraint never lets two committed rows share a value, and nothing is removed for you.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Transaction A runs in PostgreSQL at REPEATABLE READ. It totals the carts in stock; transaction B then changes one stock level and commits; A totals the carts again and then tries to change the same stock level. What happens?



A’s second total shows B’s change, and A’s update succeeds

That is READ COMMITTED, where each statement sees the data committed when the statement began.



A’s second total equals its first, and A’s update is refused, so A must try again in a new transaction

Yes. A sees the database as it was when its first statement ran, and it may not change a row that another transaction changed after that. A program at this level must be written to retry.



A’s update overwrites B’s change, since A began first

Overwriting a change A never saw is the lost update. REPEATABLE READ refuses it instead.



A’s update waits until B commits, then succeeds

B has already committed. The refusal comes because the row changed after A’s first statement.



Check Show answer Reset



3. At READ COMMITTED, a planner’s transaction runs one long SELECT SUM(quantity_on_hand) over every stock level. While the query is running, a clerk’s change to one stock level commits. What does the planner’s sum include?



Each quantity as committed when the planner’s statement began, without the clerk’s change

Yes. At READ COMMITTED each statement sees the data as committed when the statement began, so one statement’s result is consistent with itself.



The clerk’s change, since it committed before the sum finished

A statement’s view of the data is fixed when the statement begins.



Some rows before the change and some after, depending on when each row was read

The whole statement sees the data as it was committed when the statement began.



Nothing; the query is cancelled and must be run again

A commit by another transaction does not cancel a query. The query simply reads the data its view calls for.



Check Show answer Reset



4. Transaction A has updated a stock level and has not yet committed. Transaction B, at READ COMMITTED, runs an ordinary SELECT of the same row. What does B get in PostgreSQL?



A’s new quantity, since it is the latest value of the row

Reading a change that is not committed is a dirty read, and B, at READ COMMITTED, reads only committed data.



The quantity as last committed, at once, without waiting for A

Yes. PostgreSQL keeps several versions of a changed row, and a reader sees the version its snapshot calls for, so an ordinary read never waits for a write.



Nothing until A ends, since A holds a lock on the row

A’s lock makes another change of the row wait, as it does a read that locks, such as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. An ordinary read does not wait.



An error, since the row is being changed

Reading a row that another transaction is changing is allowed; the question is only which version is read.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 9 Self-Checks
text:
Security and Privileges
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A program prints a weekly report from the quality schema and changes nothing. Which practices does the chapter call for? Select every one.
Select all that apply.



Connect as a role that may only read the tables the report needs

Yes. A program connects as a role whose privileges match its job, so a mistake in it cannot change data.



Read the password from a file such as db.properties that is never committed

Yes. No password belongs in a script or in code kept under version control.



Connect as the database’s owner, so that a new table is readable at once

No program should connect as the owner or as a superuser; a mistake would then have every privilege.



Write the password into the program’s source, where it cannot be lost

Source code is shared and kept under version control, so a password in it is given to everyone who reads the code.



Check Show answer Reset



2. The role hg_sales is granted SELECT on the view production.part_catalog, but nobody has granted it anything on the schema production. A clerk acting as hg_sales queries the view. What happens?



The query succeeds, since SELECT on the view is all a query of it needs

A table or view can be reached only through its schema, which needs a privilege of its own.



The query is refused, since the role lacks USAGE on the schema

Yes. USAGE on a schema is needed to reach the objects in it at all, which is why the sales role is granted USAGE on production along with the view.



The query succeeds but returns no rows

A missing privilege refuses the statement; it never silently empties the result.



The query is refused, since a view can be granted only to its owner

Views are granted like tables; granting a view and not its table is how the chapter hides the standard cost.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Why does each sales clerk get a login role of their own, made a member of the group role hg_sales, rather than everyone logging in as one shared role?



Login roles cannot hold privileges, so a group is needed

A login role can hold privileges. The group is a matter of management, not of what roles can do.



The privileges are managed in one place, and each session still identifies the clerk who opened it

Yes. Granting or revoking a privilege on the group changes it for every member, and the database still knows who did what.



A role created NOLOGIN holds every privilege automatically

A new role has no privileges beyond those granted to everyone. NOLOGIN means only that nobody logs in as it.



A shared login is safer, since one password is easier to protect

A shared login hides who opened each session, and its password must be given to everyone who uses it.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 9 Self-Checks
text:
Review of the Whole Chapter
Read the chapter summary

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. HG Industries keeps at least 30 carts of one product across its two warehouses. A planner’s program checks the total and then takes carts from one warehouse, while another planner may do the same at the other warehouse. At which isolation level should the program’s transaction run in PostgreSQL?



READ COMMITTED, the default

The default allows both planners to read the same total and both changes to commit.



REPEATABLE READ

The two planners change different rows, so REPEATABLE READ finds nothing to refuse: a write skew.



SERIALIZABLE

Yes. PostgreSQL tracks what each transaction read and refuses a commit that no one-at-a-time order could produce. The program must retry a transaction that fails this way.



Any level, provided each program commits quickly

A short transaction makes the overlap less likely, but the same schedule can still occur, and both changes commit.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Transaction A has changed stock level 1 and now wants stock level 3, while transaction B has changed stock level 3 and now wants stock level 1. What does PostgreSQL do?



Both wait until one of the clerks cancels a transaction

Neither can proceed, but the database does not leave them waiting.



It detects the deadlock after a second or so and cancels one transaction with an error, which the program must retry

Yes. Neither transaction can proceed, so the database breaks the deadlock by cancelling one, and the program that receives the error tries its work again.



It rolls back both transactions

Cancelling one is enough to let the other go on.



It lets both changes go ahead, since each changes a different row first

Each transaction holds its lock on the row it changed until it ends, so the second change of each must wait.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Which habits does the chapter recommend for an engineer who writes reports and programs against a shared database? Select every one.
Select all that apply.



Keep transactions short, since a transaction holds its locks until it ends

Yes. A long transaction makes others wait for the rows it has changed.



Run a transaction that checks a rule across several rows before it changes one of them at SERIALIZABLE

Yes. Only that level refuses a write skew.



Write a program that uses REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE to retry a transaction that fails

Yes. At those levels PostgreSQL refuses a change it cannot make safely, and the work must be tried again.



Connect a program as the database’s owner, so that it is never refused

A program should connect as a role that may do only what its job needs, and never as the owner or a superuser.



Run every transaction at SERIALIZABLE, so that no transaction needs a retry

SERIALIZABLE is the level whose transactions may fail and need a retry, sometimes even when they would have done no harm.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 8 Self-Checks
text: These questions follow the order of Chapter 8. Each of the first six groups checks one section of the chapter, and the last group reviews the whole chapter. The “Self-check” buttons in the chapter lead to these groups. Nothing you answer is recorded.

title: Chapter 8 Self-Checks
text:
From a Design to Tables
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A colleague built a database by clicking through DataGrip’s dialogs and wants to know why the book writes every table as a statement in a script instead. Which reason is right?



A dialog creates tables by a different mechanism, which PostgreSQL cannot describe

The dialog is a convenience, not a different mechanism. It writes a CREATE statement and sends it to the server, as a script would.



A script can be read, kept under version control, and run again to rebuild the database on another machine

Yes. A script that builds a database from nothing is its most useful description. A sequence of clicks cannot be read, kept, or run again.



PostgreSQL accepts constraints only from a script

The server receives the same statements either way. The difference is what you keep afterward.



A database built from dialogs cannot be described as a script later

Both tools can generate the DDL of an existing table, which is how a database built by hand is captured as a script.



Check Show answer Reset



2. PostgreSQL keeps a search path, and SET search_path TO distribution; lets a session write customer for distribution.customer. Why do the book’s scripts still write distribution.customer in full?



PostgreSQL refuses a table name without its schema in a CREATE TABLE statement

A name without a schema is allowed; PostgreSQL looks for it in the schemas of the search path.



So that each script works whatever the search path of the session that runs it holds

Yes. A name written with its schema refers to the same table in every session, so the script does not depend on a setting it cannot see.



Because the search path holds only one schema at a time

The search path is a list of schemas, not a single one.



Because a schema’s name makes the statement run faster

The reason is that the name means the same thing everywhere, not speed.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 8 Self-Checks
text:
Data Types
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A trucking firm records the moment each load is dispatched, from terminals in three time zones, and compares dispatch times across terminals. Which type suits the column?



DATE

A date drops the time of day, which the comparison needs.



TIMESTAMP

A TIMESTAMP records a time without saying where, so 9:00 at two terminals in different zones would look like the same moment.



TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE

Yes. It records an instant, and displays it in the reader’s zone, so times from different terminals compare correctly.



VARCHAR(30), holding the time as the terminal typed it

Text sorts and compares as characters, not as moments, and two terminals may type the same time differently.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which of these values suits a DOUBLE PRECISION column?



The average time a part spends in a system, computed by a simulation model

Yes. Floating point suits a quantity that is computed rather than recorded, such as a simulation’s output.



The number of units in a production lot

A count is a whole number, so it is an INTEGER.



The date a lot was made

A calendar date is a DATE, which compares and sorts as a date.



The name of the supplier of a part

A name is text, a VARCHAR(n) or TEXT.



Check Show answer Reset



3. The order_number column is declared VARCHAR(10). What does the length limit do for the database, beyond saving space?



Nothing more; it only sets aside room for ten characters on each row

The limit is also a rule: a longer value is refused.



It acts as a small domain rule: an order number of 40 characters is a mistake, and the limit refuses it

Yes. VARCHAR(n) holds text of up to n characters and refuses a longer value, so it catches one kind of error at the door.



It pads every shorter order number with spaces to ten characters

That is what CHAR(n) does. VARCHAR(n) stores the value as given.



It requires every order number to be exactly ten characters long

The limit is a maximum. Shorter values are accepted as they are.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 8 Self-Checks
text:
Creating Tables and Constraints
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The CHECK (requested_ship_date >= order_date) of customer_order is written without a name, so PostgreSQL names it customer_order_check. When should you write CONSTRAINT some_name CHECK (...) instead?



Always, since PostgreSQL refuses a constraint without a name

PostgreSQL accepts an unnamed constraint and names it from its table and columns.



When the generated name would not tell a reader of an error message which rule was broken

Yes. Every message that reports a violation names the constraint, so a name such as order_ship_after_order points straight at the rule.



Only for a foreign key, since checks cannot be named

Any constraint can be named, a check among them.



Never, since a named constraint cannot later be removed

A named constraint is removed by its name, with ALTER TABLE ... DROP CONSTRAINT.



Check Show answer Reset



2. At stage D3, customer_order.customer_fk refers to customer. Someone runs DROP TABLE distribution.customer CASCADE. What happens to customer_order?



It is dropped too, with all its rows

The cascade removes the foreign key constraints that depend on customer, not the tables that hold them.



It remains, with its rows, but without its foreign key to customer

Yes. The cascade drops the constraints that depend on customer and then the table, so customer_fk is left as a plain column that refers to nothing.



Its customer_fk values are all set to NULL

Dropping a constraint does not change any row’s values, and customer_fk is NOT NULL besides.



The statement is refused, since another table refers to customer

A plain DROP TABLE is refused for that reason. CASCADE is what lets it go ahead.



Check Show answer Reset



3. True or False: a script that copies customers from another database can insert each customer with its old customer_pk, since the column is the primary key, by listing customer_pk in an ordinary INSERT.



True

The column is declared GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, so the database alone numbers its rows.



False

Correct. An ordinary INSERT that supplies a value for a GENERATED ALWAYS column is refused. The message’s hint names the override that a script copying rows, keys and all, would use.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 8 Self-Checks
text:
Inserting, Updating, and Deleting Rows
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A script inserts customers with INSERT INTO distribution.customer VALUES (...), leaving out the column list. It works today. What happens after a column is added to customer?



Nothing; PostgreSQL matches each value to a column by its type

Values are matched by position, not by type. Two text columns look the same to an insert.



The script breaks, or worse loads values into the wrong columns

Yes. Without a column list the values are matched to the columns in the order the table declared them, so a new column shifts the match. Always write the column list.



The new column is skipped and receives its default

That happens only when the insert lists its columns and leaves the new one out.



PostgreSQL refuses every insert without a column list

The form is allowed. It is fragile, not illegal.



Check Show answer Reset



2. True or False: on a freshly loaded stage whose last customer key is 8, an insert of a new customer is refused by a constraint and the next insert is accepted. The accepted customer receives the key 9.



True

It would, if the database numbered rows by counting them or reused a value it had handed out.



False

Correct. A generated key comes from the column’s identity counter, and an insert takes the next value even when it is refused or rolled back. The value is never given back, so the accepted customer receives 10. Look a customer’s key up by its business number rather than assuming it.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A new customer is named Crowley’s Ridge Hardware. How is the name written as a value in an INSERT?



'Crowley's Ridge Hardware'

The quote inside the name would end the value after “Crowley”, and the rest would be read as a mistake.



'Crowley''s Ridge Hardware'

Yes. A quote inside a text value is written twice, which is how SQL tells it from the quote that ends the value.



"Crowley's Ridge Hardware"

A text value is enclosed in single quotes; double quotes mean something else in SQL.



Crowley's Ridge Hardware, without quotes

A text value must be enclosed in single quotes.



Check Show answer Reset



4. An INSERT INTO distribution.customer (...) SELECT ... FROM distribution.customer_staging WHERE state = 'TX' is run, and no staged row has the state TX. What happens?



The statement is refused, since it has no rows to insert

A query that finds no rows is not an error, so nothing refuses the statement.



Nothing is inserted, and the statement reports success

Yes. That is the one danger of the INSERT ... SELECT form that the VALUES form lacks. Count the rows the query returns before relying on the insert.



One row of NULLs is inserted

An INSERT ... SELECT adds exactly the rows the query returns, here none.



PostgreSQL inserts every staged row instead

The WHERE clause chooses the rows, and it chose none.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 8 Self-Checks
text:
Loading Data from Files
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Why is a CSV file loaded into a staging table of TEXT columns without constraints, rather than straight into its final table? Select every reason that applies.
Select all that apply.



If one row broke a constraint of the final table, the whole load would be refused, and you would learn only about the first bad row

Yes. The staging table accepts anything, so every row arrives and every problem can be found with queries.



A value that is wrong but legal, such as a misspelled city, would go into the final table unnoticed

Yes. No constraint catches it; only looking at the staged rows does.



\copy cannot load a table that has constraints

\copy loads any table. The staging table is a choice made so that the rows can be examined first.



The staged rows can be repaired as they are moved, by an INSERT ... SELECT that cleans them

Yes. The move is a query, so it can trim, capitalize, and drop duplicates on the way.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A file of new customers is on your laptop, and you connect to a PostgreSQL server on another machine as an ordinary user. Which way of loading the file works?



COPY distribution.customer_staging FROM 'new-customers.csv'

COPY is run by the server and reads a file on the server’s own machine. It is also allowed only to superusers and roles granted pg_read_server_files.



psql’s \copy distribution.customer_staging FROM 'new-customers.csv' WITH (FORMAT csv, HEADER true)

Yes. \copy reads the file on your machine and sends its rows to the server, needs no special privilege, and takes the same options as COPY. The import wizards of DataGrip and DBeaver would also work.



Neither; the file must first be moved to the server

Only COPY needs the file on the server. \copy and the tools’ import wizards read it where it is.



INSERT INTO distribution.customer_staging SELECT * FROM 'new-customers.csv'

A file name is not a table, so a query cannot select from it.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Two staged rows share the customer number C-1015, but one spells the city differently. The rows are moved with INSERT INTO distribution.customer (...) SELECT DISTINCT ... FROM distribution.customer_staging. What happens?



DISTINCT keeps one of the two rows, and the load succeeds

DISTINCT removes only rows that are identical in every column, and these two differ in the city.



Both rows reach the insert, and the alternate key on customer_number refuses the whole INSERT

Yes. A duplicate with two versions needs a person to decide which is right, which is why a staging query should count the different versions of each repeated number before the move.



Both rows are inserted, and the database holds two customers numbered C-1015

customer_number is UNIQUE, so the database will not hold two.



The second row is skipped and the rest are inserted

A statement that breaks a constraint is refused as a whole; no row of it is kept.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 8 Self-Checks
text:
Changing a Table’s Definition
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The stage P1 script fills a new column of product with an UPDATE that joins it to production.part. The book also shows the standard form, which sets the column to a correlated subquery. Which form is PostgreSQL’s own?



UPDATE ... SET ... FROM production.part WHERE ...

Yes. UPDATE ... FROM joins the table being updated to another. It is PostgreSQL’s form, and both give the same result here.



UPDATE ... SET manufactured_part_fk = (SELECT ... WHERE part.part_number = product.product_number)

Setting a column to a correlated subquery is the standard form.



ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN

That adds the column. It does not fill it.



Neither; both are standard SQL

The standard has the subquery form only.



Check Show answer Reset



2. ALTER TABLE distribution.customer ADD CONSTRAINT customer_state_in_capitals CHECK (state = UPPER(state)) has been run, and every existing customer satisfies it. A later insert gives a customer the state ok. What happens?



The insert is accepted, since the constraint was added after the table was created

A constraint added to a table applies to every later change, however the table was first created.



The insert is refused, and the message names customer_state_in_capitals

Yes. The name was chosen so that the message names the rule that was broken.



The state is stored as OK

A check refuses a value; it never changes one.



The constraint is dropped, since the new row breaks it

The database keeps the rule and refuses the row.



Check Show answer Reset



3. True or False: once ALTER TABLE has added a column to the running database, the change is kept even if the database is later rebuilt from its scripts.



True

A rebuild runs the scripts, and a change that is not in them is lost.



False

Correct. Every change to a running database belongs in the scripts that rebuild it. The book’s database adds each change as a stage script that runs after the ones before it: the scripts, not the running database, are the definition.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 8 Self-Checks
text:
Review of the Whole Chapter
Read the chapter summary

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The sales department states two rules: every customer must have a city, and no two customers may share a customer number. The customer table already has customer_pk as its primary key. Which declarations implement both rules?



NOT NULL on city, and UNIQUE on customer_number

Yes. NOT NULL makes a column required, and UNIQUE declares an alternate key, so the database refuses a second customer with an existing number.



UNIQUE on city, and UNIQUE on customer_number

UNIQUE on city would stop two customers from sharing a city, which the business allows, and it does not require a city.



NOT NULL on city, and a second PRIMARY KEY on customer_number

A table has one primary key. A second identifier is an alternate key, declared UNIQUE.



NOT NULL on city, and NOT NULL on customer_number

NOT NULL requires a number but lets two customers share one.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A spreadsheet’s order dates were loaded into a text column, written as 9/2/2026 and 10/2/2026. A query sorts the orders by that column. What goes wrong?



Nothing; text sorts dates correctly in any form

Text sorts character by character, not by calendar.



10/2/2026 sorts before 9/2/2026, since the character 1 comes before 9

Yes. The type accepts the value and then misbehaves. A DATE column sorts and compares as dates.



The query is refused, since text cannot be sorted

Text can be sorted; it is sorted as text.



PostgreSQL converts the text to dates before sorting

PostgreSQL sorts a text column as text unless the query converts it.



Check Show answer Reset



3. The order_line table has primary, alternate, and foreign keys and checks on its quantity, price, and line number. Which business rule do these constraints leave unenforced?



A line may not refer to a product that does not exist

The foreign key on product_fk enforces that.



A line may not repeat a line number within its order

The alternate key on customer_order_fk and line_number enforces that.



Every order must have at least one line

Yes. The constraints check each line alone, so an order with no lines is accepted, though the class model says an order has one or more. A query must find such orders.



Deleting an order may not leave its lines behind

ON DELETE CASCADE on customer_order_fk deletes the lines with the order.

Defining Tables and Changing Data
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The customer_order table has a check named order_ship_after_order, and the business decides to drop that rule. Which statement removes it?



ALTER TABLE distribution.customer_order DROP NOT NULL

DROP NOT NULL lets one column take NULL again, and it is written with ALTER COLUMN and the column’s name. It does not remove a check.



ALTER TABLE distribution.customer_order DROP CONSTRAINT order_ship_after_order

Yes. A constraint is removed by its name, which is one reason to name a constraint when you create it.



DELETE FROM distribution.customer_order WHERE order_ship_after_order

DELETE removes rows. A constraint is part of the table’s definition, which ALTER TABLE changes.



ALTER TABLE distribution.customer_order DROP COLUMN order_ship_after_order

The constraint is not a column. DROP COLUMN removes a column and its values.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A table declares customer_fk INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES distribution.customer, naming no column of customer. Which column of customer does the foreign key refer to?



The first column of customer, whatever it is

The position of a column has nothing to do with it.



The primary key of customer

Yes. REFERENCES table with no column list refers to the table’s primary key.



Every UNIQUE column of customer, together

A foreign key refers to one key. Naming a UNIQUE column takes a column list.



None; the statement is refused without a column name

The column list may be left out, and the primary key is then assumed.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A script must start a transaction in the words of the SQL standard, so that it reads the same on another DBMS. Which statement does that?



BEGIN

PostgreSQL accepts BEGIN, and the reference lists it, but the standard’s words are different.



START TRANSACTION

Yes. START TRANSACTION begins a transaction, which COMMIT or ROLLBACK then ends.



COMMIT

COMMIT ends a transaction, keeping its changes.



SET TRANSACTION

The standard uses SET TRANSACTION to set a transaction’s isolation level, not to start one.



Check Show answer Reset

title: SQL Quick Reference Self-Checks
text:
Queries
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. An analyst combines two queries with UNION. The first selects customer_number and name; the second selects only customer_number. What happens?



The result fills the missing column with NULL

The set operations do not pad a query’s columns. Each query must supply every column.



The statement is refused, since a set operation needs the same number of columns, with compatible types, in each query

Yes. The rows of the two results are compared column by column, so the columns must line up.



Only the columns the two queries share are returned

The set operations match columns by position, not by name, and do not drop any.



The result is the same as an inner join on customer_number

A join pairs rows side by side; a set operation stacks or compares whole rows.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A report must show each order line with the total quantity of its order beside it, one row per line. How does a window function differ from GROUP BY for this?



It does not; both collapse each order’s lines into one row

GROUP BY collapses each group into one row. A window function does not.



A window function computes a value for each row from a window of related rows, without collapsing them, so every line keeps its own row

Yes. SUM(quantity) OVER (PARTITION BY ...) gives each line its order’s total while the lines stay separate.



A window function can be used only with ORDER BY and a frame

PARTITION BY alone is enough to form the windows; the ordering and the frame are optional.



A window function needs a HAVING clause to choose its rows

HAVING filters groups formed by GROUP BY; a window function needs no HAVING.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A query must run on another DBMS as well as on PostgreSQL. Which of these does the reference mark as PostgreSQL’s own, to be written differently elsewhere? Select every one.
Select all that apply.



LIMIT 10

Yes. The standard’s form is FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY.



FETCH FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY

This is the standard’s form, which PostgreSQL also accepts.



name ILIKE '%hardware%'

Yes. ILIKE matches while ignoring case; LIKE is the standard operator.



LEFT JOIN ... ON

Outer joins are standard SQL.



list_price::NUMERIC(10,2)

Yes. :: is PostgreSQL’s shorthand; the standard writes CAST(list_price AS NUMERIC(10,2)).



Check Show answer Reset

title: SQL Quick Reference Self-Checks
text:
PostgreSQL Data Types and Functions
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A report needs one text column that reads, for example, HT-100 Two-wheel hand truck, built from product_number and description. Which expression gives it?



product_number || ' ' || description

Yes. The operator || joins text, and the ' ' in the middle puts a space between the two values.



product_number + ' ' + description

In PostgreSQL, + adds numbers. Text is joined with ||.



STRING_AGG(product_number, description)

STRING_AGG joins the text values of a group of rows into one. It does not join two columns of one row.



CAST(product_number AS description)

CAST converts a value to a type, and description is a column, not a type.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A quality engineer wants the median of each characteristic’s measured values. Which aggregate from the reference gives it?



AVG(measured_value)

AVG gives the mean, which an outlying value can pull away from the middle.



PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY measured_value)

Yes. The 0.5 quantile is the median, and the values must be ordered, which is why the order is written after WITHIN GROUP.



MAX(measured_value) / 2

Half the largest value is not the middle of the values.



STDDEV_SAMP(measured_value)

That is the sample standard deviation, a measure of spread, not of the middle.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A maintenance plan records how long each planned machine stop lasts, such as 3 hours and 30 minutes. Which type from the reference holds that value?



TIME

TIME holds a time of day, such as 3:30 in the morning, not a length of time.



TIMESTAMP

A TIMESTAMP holds a date and a time, a moment rather than a duration.



INTERVAL

Yes. An INTERVAL is a length of time, and it can be added to a TIMESTAMP to find when the stop ends.



VARCHAR(20)

Stored as text, the durations could not be added, averaged, or compared.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 1 Self-Checks
section: From Files and Spreadsheets to Databases
text:
From Files and Spreadsheets to Databases
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A hardware store opens an account with HG Industries in December, weeks before it places its first order. The sales office still keeps its orders in the order log, one row per order line. Which problem does the request to record the new store run into?



Changing a fact

Nothing recorded about the store needs to change; the store is not in the log at all yet.



Recording a fact on its own

Yes. Every row of the log is a line of an order, so a customer with no order has no row to live in. The same problem keeps a new product out of the log until someone orders it.



Removing a fact

Removing a fact is the opposite trouble: deleting an order’s only row also deletes what the log knew about its customer.



Keeping the rules

The rules concern values typed wrongly, such as a quantity of ten. Here the value is fine; there is simply no place for it.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Why does the order log store most of its facts many times?



Because the clerks copy rows by mistake

The copies are not mistakes. They follow from what a row of the log is.



Because each row mixes facts about four things: an order, a customer, a product, and one product’s quantity and price on one order

Yes. A customer’s city is written on every line of every order the customer places, and a product’s description on every line that orders it. Nothing ties the copies together.



Because a spreadsheet cannot hold more than one sheet

A workbook can hold many sheets. The trouble is how the facts are arranged within a row, not how many sheets there are.



Because the log records orders in the order they were taken

The order of the rows has nothing to do with how often a fact is repeated.



Check Show answer Reset



3. In HG Industries’ database, which of these bad entries does the chapter say the database refuses only if it is told to?



An order line for a product number that does not exist

The chapter lists this among the entries the database refuses, since an order line refers to a product rather than copying it.



A quantity that is not a number

The chapter lists this among the entries the database refuses without being asked.



An order date in 2062

Yes. A date far in the future is still a date. The database refuses it only when a rule says what range of dates is sensible.



None; the database refuses every bad entry on its own

A database enforces the rules stored with the data. A rule nobody declared is not enforced.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 1 Self-Checks
text:
Industrial Data and Database Systems
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Which of these are analytical uses of HG Industries’ records? Select every one that is.
Select all that apply.



The average weekly demand for the HT-100 over the past year

Yes. It summarizes many orders to see a pattern.



Looking up whether order SO-5004 has shipped

This is operational: one event of the business, looked up as it happens.



The fraction of a carrier’s shipments that arrived on time, by month

Yes. It summarizes many shipments over time.



Recording the coating thickness measured on a lot as it is inspected

This is operational: one inspection, recorded as it happens.



Check Show answer Reset

The same records serve both kinds of use, but the two ask different things of a database.




2. An engineer queries HG Industries’ database in DataGrip, while a scheduling application written for the plant reads the same database. How does each reach the data?



Each opens the database’s files directly and reads the rows it needs

People and programs do not open a database directly. The DBMS stores the rows and finds them.



Both communicate with the DBMS in SQL, and the DBMS finds the rows each asks for

Yes. Tools and programs alike send SQL to the DBMS, which does the work of storing and finding the data.



DataGrip uses SQL, but a program needs a language of its own to reach the data

A program written for a purpose uses SQL to reach the database, just as a tool does.



The application reads a copy that DataGrip exports for it

Both use the same database through the DBMS. Nothing needs copying.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Suppose a plant’s database is extended to record the maintenance of each machine. Which of these is metadata rather than data? Select every one that is.
Select all that apply.



The table of machines has a column for the date of the last maintenance, of a date type

Yes. It describes what the database can hold, not any machine.



Every maintenance record must name a machine that exists

Yes. A rule the data must obey is stored in the catalog with the description of the tables.



One welder was last maintained on a given date

This is a fact about one machine: data, not data about the data.



The number of maintenance records entered last week

This counts data. It is a fact computed from the records, not a description of them.



Check Show answer Reset



4. HG Industries records that order SO-5001 shipped with Boston Mountain Freight three days early. Which decisions use records of this kind? Select every one that does.
Select all that apply.



Choosing a carrier

Yes. Shipments, carriers, and delivery dates are logistics records, and carrier selection uses them.



Measuring on-time performance

Yes. Summarized over many shipments, the same records show how often orders ship on time.



Setting safety stock for a warehouse

Safety stock is decided from inventory records: items, locations, stock levels, and reorder points.



Planning the capacity of the frame line

Capacity planning uses production records, such as routings, work centers, and work orders.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 1 Self-Checks
section: From a Model to a Database
text:
From a Model to a Database
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Once the class model of a business is settled, which step of implementing turns it into tables with keys that link them?



Mapping

Yes. Mapping turns the classes and their associations into tables, and the keys connect the tables as the associations connected the classes.



Normalization

Normalization comes after mapping. It checks the tables so that each fact is stored once.



Querying

Queries use the tables once they exist and hold data.



Drawing the class diagram

The class diagram is the model itself, which this step starts from.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A reader writes a query meant to list each customer in the base data of HG Industries’ database once. It returns eleven rows. What should the reader conclude?



Nothing; the computer’s answer is the answer

The point of a small database is that you need not take the computer’s word for it.



The query is wrong, since the base data holds eight customers, and a list of each customer once cannot be longer than that

Yes. The base data is kept small on purpose so that you can check any query’s answer by hand. Here the check fails before the result reaches anyone else.



Three customers were added since the chapter was written

The base data holds eight customers. The customers that the year of history adds belong to a later stage, not to the base data.



The database is too small to give a reliable answer

A small database gives exact answers. Its size is what makes a wrong one easy to see.



Check Show answer Reset



3. An engineer is asked to build a database for a machine shop’s tool crib and begins by sketching tables and choosing data types. What does the chapter advise first?



Load a sample of the crib’s records and let the tables follow from them

Records show what happened to be written down, not what the business needs to record.



Settle what the business records, and how those things are related, before deciding how to store them

Yes. That is modeling, done independently of any software. Tables, keys, and types are implementation, answered by the model.



Choose the DBMS, since the tables depend on it

The model does not depend on any software, and the choice of DBMS comes after it.



Write the queries the crib attendant will run, then create the tables they need

Queries use a database that exists. What the database must hold comes first.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 1 Self-Checks
text:
Review of the Whole Chapter
Read the chapter summary

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. In HG Industries’ database, order SO-5002 is canceled and its order removed. What happens to what the database knows about Cedar Creek Home Center?



It is lost, since the order was the only place the customer appeared

That is what happened in the spreadsheet log. The database records each customer once, in a table of customers, apart from its orders.



It remains, because the customer is recorded in its own table and the order only refers to it

Yes. Removing the order removes the order, not the customer.



It is copied into a backup table automatically

Nothing needs copying. The customer’s row was never part of the order.



The database refuses to remove the order while the customer exists

A customer may exist with no orders, just as a product may exist before anyone orders it.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which problems of the order log appear only once more than one person needs it? Select every one that does.
Select all that apply.



Two clerks edit their own copies of the file on the same afternoon, and one clerk’s work is lost when the other’s is saved

Yes. Sharing one file between people produces competing versions.



A question that crosses the log and the warehouse’s own spreadsheet of stock means copying and matching rows by hand

Yes. Each department’s file answers its own questions; a question that spans two files has no place to be asked.



A customer’s move must be recorded on every one of its rows

This trouble arises even if one clerk keeps the log alone. It comes from storing the city many times.



A new product cannot be recorded before anyone orders it

This arises with a single user too. It comes from what a row of the log is.



Check Show answer Reset



3. The production department keeps a parts list in its own spreadsheet, and the quality department keeps another, both listing the same frame. Why does the chapter argue for one database instead?



Each department’s spreadsheet is too small to hold its parts

Size is not the issue; a parts list fits in a spreadsheet easily.



The functions share their data, so separate copies store each fact many times and can drift apart

Yes. The part that production makes is the part that quality inspects. The records of an industrial system form one connected body of data, and a database should connect them too.



Quality records are analytical and production records are operational

Both departments record individual events as they happen, and both records can also be summarized.



Only a database can store a part’s description

A spreadsheet can store a description. The trouble is storing it twice with nothing to keep the copies the same.



Check Show answer Reset
