title: Chapter 3 Self-Checks
section: The SELECT Statement and Filtering Rows
text:
The SELECT Statement and Filtering Rows
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A query looks up a customer with the condition WHERE customer_number = "C-1001". What happens?



It finds Riverside Hardware, since single and double quotes mean the same thing

They do not. A text value is written in single quotes, and double quotes mark a name.



PostgreSQL refuses it, since double quotes mark a name, so the condition asks for a column named C-1001

Yes. Written 'C-1001', in single quotes, the value is text, and the query finds the customer.



It returns no rows, since no customer number contains quotation marks

The double quotes are not read as part of a value at all. They make C-1001 the name of a column.



It finds Riverside Hardware, since customer_number is an alternate key

Being a key does not change how a value must be written in a condition.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A query names only product_number and description after SELECT, and its condition is WHERE list_price < 125. What does it return?



Nothing; PostgreSQL refuses a condition on a column that the SELECT list does not name

The condition is allowed. The WHERE clause sees every column of the table.



The number and description of each product priced under $125

Yes. The condition is evaluated on the whole row, whether or not the SELECT list names the column it tests.



The number, description, and list price of each product priced under $125

The result has only the columns the SELECT list names. Testing a column does not add it to the result.



Every product, since the condition’s column is not shown

Showing a column and testing it are separate. The rows are still filtered by price.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Which product numbers does the condition product_number LIKE 'GC-_00' match? Select every one it does.
Select all that apply.



GC-300

Yes. The _ stands for exactly one character, here the 3.



GC-400

Yes. Any one character may stand where the _ is.



GC-3000

The pattern has exactly six characters, and the _ matches one character only. This number has seven.



HT-100

The pattern begins with GC-, which must match exactly.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 3 Self-Checks
text:
NULL and Three-Valued Logic
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A work order is still in process, so its completed_on is NULL. Its due_on is a date in the past. What is the value of the condition completed_on > due_on for this work order?



True, because the work order is overdue

The work order is overdue, but this condition compares the completion date, which is unknown.



False, because a NULL counts as no date at all

NULL is not treated as zero or as an empty value. A comparison with NULL has a third value.



Unknown

Yes. A comparison in which either side is NULL is neither true nor false; it is unknown. A WHERE clause discards the row, just as it would discard a false one.



The query stops with an error

Comparing with NULL is allowed. It gives an answer, just not true or false.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Work order WO-7008 is open, so its completed_on is NULL, and it was due on March 13, 2026. What is the value of completed_on > due_on OR due_on < DATE '2026-03-20' for it?



True

Yes. The first part is unknown and the second is true, and true OR anything is true, whatever the unknown turns out to be.



Unknown, since one part of the condition is unknown

An unknown part makes an OR unknown only when the other part is not true. Here the other part is true.



False, since the work order has no completion date

A missing completion date makes the first comparison unknown, not false, and the second part is true anyway.



The query stops with an error

Combining unknown with OR is allowed, and the truth table of OR gives its value.



Check Show answer Reset



3. The query for the work orders that are late as of March 20, 2026 writes the date DATE '2026-03-20' into its condition. What should change if the plant manager wants the same list every morning?



Nothing; the query finds the late work orders whenever it runs

With the date written in, the query answers the question as of March 20 only.



Replace the written date with CURRENT_DATE, the date on which the query runs

Yes. The open work orders due before today are late today, so the comparison must move with the day.



Remove the date, and keep only completed_on > due_on

That condition misses every open work order, since it is unknown whenever completed_on is NULL.



Add ORDER BY due_on

Sorting changes the order of the rows, not which rows count as late.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 3 Self-Checks
text:
Sorting, Limiting, and Expressions
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A query ends with ORDER BY warehouse_fk, quantity_on_hand DESC. In what order does it list the stock levels?



Both columns from largest to smallest

DESC applies only to the column it follows. Each column is sorted on its own terms.



By warehouse from smallest to largest, and within each warehouse from the largest quantity on hand to the smallest

Yes. The first column sorts the rows, the second breaks the ties within it, and only the second is descending.



By quantity on hand from largest to smallest, and then by warehouse

The columns sort in the order they are named, so the warehouse comes first.



By warehouse, with the quantities in no particular order

The second column breaks the ties of the first, so the quantities within each warehouse are sorted.



Check Show answer Reset



2. For a work order still in process, completed_on is NULL. What does the expression completed_on - released_on give for it, and what does COALESCE(completed_on, DATE '2026-03-20') - released_on give?



Zero, and the days from release to March 20

NULL is not zero, so the first expression is not zero.



NULL, and the days from release to March 20

Yes. Any arithmetic with a NULL operand gives NULL. COALESCE returns the first of its arguments that is not NULL, so it substitutes March 20 for the missing date.



An error, and the days from release to March 20

Arithmetic with NULL is allowed; it gives NULL.



NULL, and NULL

COALESCE replaces the NULL before the subtraction, so the second expression has a value.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Two orders have no requested ship date. A query ends with ORDER BY requested_ship_date. Where does PostgreSQL put those two orders?



First, since NULL is smaller than any date

PostgreSQL does the opposite in ascending order.



Last, since PostgreSQL sorts NULL as if it were larger than every value

Yes. They come last in ascending order and first in descending order. The SQL standard leaves the choice to each database, so writing NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST makes the query’s meaning plain anywhere.



Nowhere: rows with a NULL in the ORDER BY column are left out

Sorting never removes rows. Only WHERE, a join condition, or LIMIT can do that.



In whatever order they happen to be stored

The two orders do move as a block to one end; only their order relative to each other is left to any further ORDER BY columns.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 3 Self-Checks
text:
Inner Joins
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. We evaluate a join by hand on three customers and the four orders that two of them placed. How many pairs does the cross product hold, before the join condition is applied?



4

Four is the number of pairs the join condition keeps, one for each order. The cross product comes first.



7

The cross product multiplies the row counts; it does not add them.



12

Yes. Every one of the 3 customers is paired with every one of the 4 orders, \(3 \times 4 = 12\), and the join condition then keeps the pairs whose keys match.



3

Every customer appears in the cross product, but each is paired with every order.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A query joins product, order_line, customer_order, and customer, one JOIN at a time. How many join conditions does it need?



One, naming all four tables

Each JOIN adds one table and the condition that connects it to a table already joined.



Three

Yes. A join of four tables needs three conditions, one for each foreign key along the path from product to customer.



Four, one for each table

The first table needs no condition; each table joined after it needs one.



Six, one for each pair of tables

Only tables connected by a foreign key are matched. Each condition follows one foreign key line of the schema.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A join can be written with both tables in FROM, separated by a comma, and the join condition in WHERE, or with JOIN and ON. Why does the book use the JOIN form? Select every reason it gives.
Select all that apply.



It keeps each join condition beside the table it joins, which makes a query of several tables easier to read

Yes. The conditions that connect tables stand apart from the conditions that filter rows.



The outer joins can be written no other way

Yes. A left join needs ON to say what counts as a match.



It returns different rows from the comma form

The two forms mean the same thing and return the same rows.



It makes the database build the cross product first

The database never actually builds the cross product, in either form. The cross product is how to think about a join.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 3 Self-Checks
text:
Outer Joins
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A warehouse takes a physical count of its stock and wants to compare it with the stock levels on record. Either list may hold products that the other lacks. Which join suits the comparison?



An inner join

An inner join keeps only the products in both lists, which hides exactly the differences the comparison is for.



A left join from the count to the stock levels

This keeps every counted product, but a stock level that the count missed is left out.



A full join

Yes. A FULL JOIN keeps the unmatched rows of both tables, padded with NULL, so a product missing from either list appears.



A right join from the count to the stock levels

A right join keeps every row of the table named after it, so it misses the counted products with no stock level on record.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Customer 8, Northgate Hardware, has placed no orders. In the result of customer AS c LEFT JOIN customer_order AS o ON o.customer_fk = c.customer_pk, what does Northgate Hardware’s row hold?



Nothing: the customer has no row, since it matched no order

That is what an inner join does. A left join adds back the unmatched rows of its left-hand table.



The customer’s own columns, and NULL in every column that would have come from customer_order

Yes. The outer join supplies the NULLs; the customer’s own data comes from its table as before. Testing one of those NULL columns is how a left join finds the customers with no orders.



The customer’s columns, and the values of the most recent order of any customer

The left join pairs a row only with rows that satisfy the join condition, and none does.



One row for each order in the table, each marked as not matching

Rows that do not match are not paired at all; the customer appears once, padded with NULL.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A report must list every warehouse, with its stock levels where it has any. Which FROM clauses keep a warehouse that has no stock levels?
Select all that apply.



warehouse AS w LEFT JOIN stock_level AS s ON s.warehouse_fk = w.warehouse_pk

Yes. The table named before LEFT JOIN is the one whose rows are all kept.



stock_level AS s LEFT JOIN warehouse AS w ON s.warehouse_fk = w.warehouse_pk

This keeps every stock level, but a warehouse with none matches no stock level and is left out.



warehouse AS w JOIN stock_level AS s ON s.warehouse_fk = w.warehouse_pk

An inner join returns only matched rows.



stock_level AS s RIGHT JOIN warehouse AS w ON w.warehouse_pk = s.warehouse_fk

Yes. A right join keeps every row of the table named after it, here warehouse, so it is the left join above written the other way round. The book writes every outer join as a left join, which reads in the order of the request.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 3 Self-Checks
text:
Subqueries
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A query keeps the products for which EXISTS (SELECT * FROM distribution.stock_level AS s WHERE s.product_fk = p.product_pk AND s.quantity_on_hand <= s.reorder_point) holds. Which statements about the EXISTS test are true? Select every one that is.
Select all that apply.



It is true for a product when the subquery returns at least one row, and false when it returns none

Yes. EXISTS tests only whether a row exists, so it is never unknown.



Writing SELECT 1 or SELECT s.warehouse_fk in place of SELECT * would not change the result

Yes. The select list of an EXISTS subquery does not matter; SELECT * is only the convention.



The subquery is run once for the whole query, not for each product

It refers to p.product_pk, the outer row, so it is read as being run once for each product.



A product short in both warehouses appears twice

The outer query reads the product table, and the test is true or false once for each product, so each appears at most once.



Check Show answer Reset



2. In a subquery, a column is named without its table’s alias, and the subquery’s own table has no column of that name, though the outer query’s table does. What happens?



PostgreSQL refuses the query

It would refuse a qualified name, such as o.customer_pk. An unqualified name is looked up further out.



The name refers to the outer query’s table, and the subquery becomes correlated by accident

Yes. The query runs and gives a wrong answer rather than a message. That is why every column in a subquery should be named with its table’s alias.



The column is treated as NULL

The name is resolved to a real column, just not the one intended.



The subquery returns no rows

It returns rows, from the outer row’s own column.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A query keeps the products priced above one product’s price, looked up by a subquery:
WHERE list_price > (SELECT list_price
                    FROM distribution.product
                    WHERE product_number = 'HT-900')
No product has the number HT-900. What does the query return?



Every product, since there is no price to exceed

The subquery does have a value; it is just not a price.



No rows, since the subquery’s value is NULL and every comparison with it is unknown

Yes. A subquery used as a single value returns NULL when it finds no row. Had it found several rows, PostgreSQL would have stopped with an error instead. Looking the product up by its alternate key guarantees at most one row.



An error, since the subquery returns no rows

PostgreSQL stops with an error only when such a subquery returns more than one row.



The most expensive product

Nothing in the query compares the products with one another.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 3 Self-Checks
section: Set Operations and Common Table Expressions
text:
Set Operations and Common Table Expressions
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A UNION of the customers’ cities and states and the warehouses’ cities and states ends with ORDER BY state, city. What does the ORDER BY sort?



Only the rows of the second query, the warehouses

The ORDER BY follows the second query, but it does not belong to it.



The combined result of both queries

Yes. An ORDER BY at the end of a set operation sorts the result that the operation produces.



Each query’s rows separately, the customers’ and then the warehouses’

The union is one result, and it is sorted as one.



Nothing, since a set operation cannot be sorted

A union is a result like any other, and an ORDER BY sorts it.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which statement about a common table expression that does not refer to itself is true?



It stores its result in the database for later queries

A CTE exists only while its statement runs.



It can answer requests that no subquery can

It could be written as a subquery in the FROM clause instead.



It names a step of a long query, which the rest of the statement uses like a table

Yes. What it adds is readability: each step can be named for what it means, and run and checked on its own.



It must be the last part of the statement

A CTE comes first, introduced by WITH; the statement that uses it follows.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 3 Self-Checks
text:
Review of the Whole Chapter
Read the chapter summary

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A request reads “the number, description, and list price of each product under $125, cheapest first”. Which clauses does its query need besides SELECT and FROM?



WHERE only

“Cheapest first” says in what order, which is a clause of its own.



WHERE and ORDER BY

Yes. “Under $125” says which rows, and “cheapest first” says in what order. Reading a request clause by clause tells you which clauses its query needs before you write any of them.



ORDER BY and LIMIT

“Under $125” is a condition on each row, not a count of rows.



GROUP BY and HAVING

Nothing in the request divides the products into groups.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A query finds the products that have never been ordered by joining product AS p LEFT JOIN order_line AS l ON l.product_fk = p.product_pk and keeping the rows where a column is NULL. Which test should it use?



l.order_line_pk IS NULL

Yes. A real order line always has a primary key, so a NULL there can come only from the left join’s padding.



p.product_pk IS NULL

Every row’s product columns come from the product table itself, and its key is never NULL, so this keeps no rows.



l.order_line_pk IS NOT NULL

This keeps the products that matched an order line: those that have been ordered.



p.list_price IS NULL

A product’s own columns say nothing about whether it matched an order line.



Check Show answer Reset

The test must use a column that cannot be NULL in a matched row. Otherwise a product that was ordered could look unordered.




3. Before running a new query, why evaluate it by hand on a few rows?



The database needs the predicted rows to check its own answer

The database knows nothing of our prediction.



The prediction, compared with the result, catches a wrong condition, a lost NULL, or fan-out before the result reaches a report

Yes. Write down what each step produces, then run the query; its result must match. The habit also builds the understanding that makes a long query readable.



Hand evaluation is faster than running the query

It is slower. Its value is the check it gives, not speed.



Only queries with joins need it

Conditions with NULL, AND and OR, and LIMIT with ties all reward the same check.



Check Show answer Reset

title: NoSQL Self-Checks
section: Why NoSQL Databases Exist and the Four Families
text:
Why NoSQL Databases Exist and the Four Families
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Why does a key-value store often sit in front of another database?



It returns a value very fast when given its key, so it can hold the answers to frequent questions while the other database holds the facts

Yes. Its speed comes from its simplicity: it stores a value under a key and does not look inside it.



It checks each change against the other database’s rules before passing it on

A key-value store checks nothing; it does not even look inside the values it holds.



It can answer any question the other database can, only faster

It finds a record by its key and nothing else. Questions about the values need another database.



It keeps the history that the other database discards

A key-value store holds a value per key. Keeping years of history is the work of a historian or a warehouse.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which question can a document database answer that a key-value store cannot?



Return the record stored under order number SO-5001

Both can do that. Finding a record by its key is all a key-value store does.



Find every order whose lines include a GC-300

Yes. A document database looks inside its documents and can search by the values of their fields. A key-value store does not look inside the value it holds.



Return a value very fast when given its key

Both find a record by its key. Speed at that is the key-value store’s strength, not a question only the document database can answer.



Store records too large for one machine

Spreading data over many machines is one of the needs behind NoSQL in general, not a difference between these two families.



Check Show answer Reset



3. True or False: a plant historian holds an oven’s temperatures along with the plant’s lots and work orders, so a question such as “the temperatures during the runs of one lot that failed inspection” is answered inside the historian.



True

A historian holds tags measured over time. It does not hold orders, parts, or work orders.



False

Correct. The usual design summarizes the readings, such as each tag’s average, minimum, and maximum over each hour or run, and loads the summaries into a relational database, where they join the rest of the plant’s data.



Check Show answer Reset

title: NoSQL Self-Checks
text:
The Trade-offs
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A document database applies schema on read. What is its main cost?



The database refuses any document whose fields differ from the others in its collection

That would be schema on write. A document database usually stores whatever document it is given.



Every program that reads the data must cope with every shape that has ever been written, including the mistakes

Yes. The program decides what the fields mean, so a misspelled field is accepted when written and can make a later query answer wrongly.



The structure cannot change without redesigning the database

That is the cost schema on read avoids: the structure can change without a redesign.



The documents cannot be searched by their fields

A document database can search by the values of fields. The trouble is that nothing guarantees which fields are there.



Check Show answer Reset



2. True or False: a document database can never check the fields of the documents it stores, since schema on read is all it offers.



True

Many document databases now let a designer declare rules that documents must obey.



False

Correct. Declared rules move a document database part of the way back to schema on write. Without them, it stores whatever document it is given.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A NoSQL database keeps several copies of each record and offers eventual consistency. For which use is a read from a copy that has not yet received the latest change most likely to do harm?



A dashboard showing each machine’s state, refreshed every second

A value a second old does no harm on a dashboard.



The quantity on hand of a part that two planners are allocating at the same time

Yes. Each planner may allocate from a value the other has already used. Many NoSQL databases let a program ask for stronger consistency on the operations that need it, at the cost of speed.



A log of sensor readings that are written once and never changed

Readings that never change are read back the same from any copy once they have arrived.



A report of last year’s sales, run once a month

Last year’s figures are no longer changing, so a short delay between copies does not matter to them.



Check Show answer Reset

title: NoSQL Self-Checks
text:
Documents in PostgreSQL
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The query of January’s orders filters with WHERE document ->> 'order_date' < '2026-02-01'. Why does the comparison give the right orders?



->> returns text, and dates written in the form 2026-01-05 sort as text in the same order as dates

Yes. The comparison is of text, and it works only because of the form the dates were written in.



->> returns the field as a DATE, since PostgreSQL recognizes the date

->> always returns text. Nothing in the document declares the field a date.



PostgreSQL compares any two strings as dates when both look like dates

PostgreSQL compares two strings as text. The form of these dates makes text order and date order agree.



The comparison would give the right orders whatever form the dates were written in

Dates written in another form, such as month first, need not sort as text in date order.



Check Show answer Reset



2. The condition document @> '{"lines": [{"product_number": "GC-300"}]}' is applied to each order document. Which documents does it keep?



Those whose list of lines includes a line for the GC-300, whatever that line’s other fields

Yes. @> asks whether a document contains another, and a line with more fields still contains the one field asked for.



Those whose only line is for the GC-300

Containment does not require the list to hold nothing else. An order with other lines as well is kept.



Those whose GC-300 line has no field but its product number

Containment ignores the fields the condition does not name.



None; @> compares whole documents for equality

Equality would need the whole document to match. @> asks only whether the document contains the one given.



Check Show answer Reset

title: NoSQL Self-Checks
text:
Choosing
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A plant runs a historian on the floor, a relational database for orders and production, and a warehouse for analysis, each for the data it suits. What is this practice called?



Polyglot persistence

Yes. A plant’s information systems usually practice it, and each of the databases still answers the two questions of where the description of the data lives and how records connect.



Eventual consistency

Eventual consistency concerns copies of one record that may briefly disagree, not the use of several kinds of database.



Schema on read

Schema on read concerns when a document’s structure is applied, not how many kinds of database a system uses.



Denormalization

Denormalization repeats facts within one design. Using several databases, each for its own data, is a different matter.



Check Show answer Reset



2. True or False: the designer of a NoSQL database usually starts from the business and lets the questions come later, as the designer of a relational database does.



True

A key-value store finds a record only by its key, and combining collections is often left to the program, so the records must be shaped for known questions.



False

Correct. A NoSQL design starts from the questions known in advance. A relational database answers any question its data can answer, which matters to an engineer whose next question is rarely the last one.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 6 Self-Checks
section: The Mapping Process and Mapping Classes
text:
The Mapping Process and Mapping Classes
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A designer maps the classes of a model one at a time: the first class with its attributes, keys, and associations, then the second, and so on. Why does the mapping instead apply each step to the whole model before taking the next step?



Because PostgreSQL creates tables only in alphabetical order

The order of the steps has nothing to do with how the database creates tables. It comes from what each step needs.



Because a later step needs the tables and keys that the earlier steps produce

Yes. An association cannot become a foreign key until the table it refers to exists and has its primary key, so all the classes and their keys come first.



Because the class model may be changed only between steps

The class model may be revised whenever a check shows it is wrong, not only between steps.



Because each step produces a separate database

All the steps produce one relational schema, built up step by step.



Check Show answer Reset



2. The class ManufacturedPart has an attribute lotSize. What are the table and the column called?



Table ManufacturedPart, column lotSize

Tables and columns are named in snake_case, not in the capitalized style of class and attribute names.



Table manufactured_part, column lot_size

Yes. Each name is written in snake_case, and the table keeps the singular of the class, since it implements a class that describes one object.



Table manufactured_parts, column lot_size

The table is named in the singular, like the class it implements.



Table part, column manufactured_lot_size

A class maps to a table named for that class, not for another.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A hypothetical Supplier class has a business identifier supplierNumber, a name, and a minimumOrderValue that must be positive. Which of these does mapping the class give the supplier table? Select every one that does.
Select all that apply.



A UNIQUE constraint on supplier_number

Yes. The business promises that no two suppliers share a number, so the column is an alternate key.



A CHECK that minimum_order_value is greater than zero

Yes. No SQL type holds only positive amounts, so a CHECK implements the narrower domain.



A primary key that the class model does not name

Yes. A class model names no identifier; the mapping supplies one, under the book’s convention a surrogate key supplier_pk.



A name column that allows NULL, since names are free text

Free text is a type, not a multiplicity. With no [0..1] on the attribute, the column is NOT NULL.



A UNIQUE constraint on minimum_order_value

Two suppliers may well have the same minimum. Only a value the business promises is never shared becomes a key.



Check Show answer Reset



4. In the last step of the mapping, a designer puts a few objects and links from a cloud instance diagram into the new tables as rows, and the rows cannot hold what the diagram shows. What should the designer do?



Add columns to the tables until the rows fit

Patching the tables hides the problem. A table that cannot hold the diagram’s links says that the model or the mapping is wrong.



Remove the objects that do not fit from the diagram

The diagram shows what the business records. Dropping the objects that do not fit throws away a requirement.



Go back to the class model, and to the mapping, to find what is wrong

Yes. A check that fails sends the designer back to the class model, and the diagram shows where the trouble is. When a mapping seems hard, the trouble is usually in the model, not the rules.



Nothing, since a check that fails is expected the first time

A failed check is a finding, not a formality. The tables would lose or contradict data.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 6 Self-Checks
text:
Mapping Associations
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Each work order is for exactly one part, and a part may have any number of work orders: Part 1 -- 0..* WorkOrder. How does the association map?



A column work_order_fk in part

A part may have many work orders, so its row cannot hold its links as a single value. This puts the foreign key on the wrong side.



A column part_fk in work_order, NOT NULL

Yes. A one-to-many association maps to a foreign key in the table of the many end, and the minimum of 1 at the Part end makes it NOT NULL.



A column part_fk in work_order that allows NULL

The side is right, but the 1 at the Part end has a minimum of one: every work order has its part.



A table of its own holding part_fk and work_order_fk

A table of its own is needed only when neither end can hold its links as one value. Here each work order has exactly one part.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Customer 1 -- 0..* CustomerOrder maps to the foreign key customer_fk in customer_order, NOT NULL. What does the 0..* at the CustomerOrder end add to the tables?



A column in customer that counts the customer’s orders

A count can be computed from the orders whenever it is wanted; storing it would record a fact twice.



A CHECK that allows a customer to have no orders

No check is needed to allow something the tables already allow.



Nothing: a customer with no orders is a customer whose key appears in no order’s customer_fk

Yes. A minimum of zero and a maximum of many are what a foreign key at the many end allows by itself.



A foreign key in customer to its orders, which may be NULL

A customer may have many orders, so its row cannot hold its links as one value.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A hypothetical operator table records each operator’s lead in lead_fk, a foreign key to operator_pk in the same table. How does a query find the crew of a given lead?



By reading a list of crew members stored in the lead’s row

A lead may have any number of crew members, so the lead’s row cannot hold them as one value. It holds only its own lead.



By selecting the rows whose lead_fk is the lead’s key

Yes. A lead’s crew is found from the other side, just as a customer’s orders are the rows whose customer_fk is the customer’s key.



By following lead_fk from the lead’s own row

The lead’s own lead_fk leads up, to the lead’s lead, not down to the crew.



It cannot, without a second table of crews

The one foreign key records every link. The crew is read from the rows that point to the lead.



Check Show answer Reset



4. Both ends of a one-to-one association are 1, and the two objects are always created and removed together. Besides a UNIQUE foreign key on one side, which mapping does the chapter offer?



Two foreign keys, one in each table, each referring to the other

Two foreign keys record each link twice and can disagree.



One table that holds the attributes of both classes, with no foreign key

Yes. When the two objects come and go together, nothing is lost by storing them in one row.



A table of its own for the association, holding two foreign keys

A table of its own is the choice for two 0..1 ends, where a foreign key on either side would often be NULL.



No mapping, since a relational table cannot record a one-to-one association

A one-to-one association maps readily, by a UNIQUE foreign key or, here, by one table.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 6 Self-Checks
text:
Mapping Qualified Associations
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. In the mapping of the order line, the alternate key (customer_order_fk, line_number) keeps the qualifier’s meaning in the tables. Which rule of class models does the chapter call it the order line’s version of?



The rule that every attribute without a multiplicity has exactly one value

That rule decides which columns are NOT NULL, not which are keys.



The rule that one association holds at most one link between a given pair of objects

Yes. Here the pair is an order and a line number, and the key allows at most one line for each pair.



The rule that a composition’s part cannot outlive its whole

That rule decides what a deletion does to the foreign key, not which columns form a key.



The rule that a subclass inherits everything the superclass has

Inheritance concerns generalization, which an order line does not take part in.



Check Show answer Reset



2. The construct-by-construct ledger of the refined order model maps classes, business identifiers, attributes, and associations. One column of the resulting order_line table has no row of that ledger to come from. Which one, and why?



unit_price, since a price is computed rather than recorded

The unit price is an attribute of OrderLine, recorded for each line, and the ledger maps it with the other attributes.



line_number, since the line number is a qualifier of the association, not an attribute of OrderLine

Yes. The ledger leaves it for the mapping of qualified associations, where it becomes part of a key.



product_fk, since a foreign key is not part of a class model

The association between OrderLine and Product has its row in the ledger, and product_fk is its result.



order_line_pk, since the class model names no identifier

The ledger’s first row gives every table its surrogate key, order_line_pk among them.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A qualified association is mapped in which step of the mapping process?



Step 1, since the qualifier names a class

A qualifier belongs to an association; it does not name a class of its own.



Step 3, since every key is chosen in the step that gives each table its identity

Step 3 gives each table its primary key and its business identifiers as alternate keys. The qualifier’s key comes with its association.



Step 4, the mapping of each association

Yes. A qualified association is an association, so it is mapped with the others, after the classes and their keys exist.



Step 7, the check of the tables

Step 7 checks the tables the earlier steps built. It maps nothing new.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 6 Self-Checks
text:
Mapping Generalization
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The parts are mapped with a table for each class: part holds part_number and description, and manufactured_part holds lot_size. A report needs the part number and lot size of every manufactured part. What does its query need?



Nothing more than manufactured_part, since a subclass holds its inherited attributes

In this mapping the inherited attributes stay in the superclass table. A manufactured part is split across two tables.



A join of the two tables on part_number

part_number is not a column of manufactured_part. The subclass table holds only its own attributes and the shared key.



A join of manufactured_part to part on the shared key, part_fk equal to part_pk

Yes. The subclass table’s primary key, part_fk, is also its foreign key to part, so a manufactured part has the same key value in both tables, and the join puts the whole object back together.



A left join from part, so that purchased parts appear with a NULL lot size

That lists every part, not the manufactured parts the report asks for.



Check Show answer Reset



2. True or False: with a table for each class, the database refuses a part that has a row in both manufactured_part and purchased_part.



True

Each subclass table’s foreign key checks only that the part exists. Nothing compares the two subclass tables.



False

Correct. This mapping does not keep {disjoint, complete}: a part may be in both subclass tables, or in neither. A checking query finds such parts after the fact; it does not prevent them.



Check Show answer Reset



3. In the mapping of a generalization to one table, the column part_kind holds manufactured or purchased for each row. What is such a column called?



A discriminator

Yes. A discriminator says which subclass each row belongs to, so that one table can hold the objects of every subclass.



A qualifier

A qualifier belongs to an association end. part_kind belongs to each row of the table itself.



A surrogate key

A surrogate key identifies a row. Many rows share each value of part_kind.



A foreign key

part_kind holds a word, not a reference to another table’s key.



Check Show answer Reset



4. True or False: the one-table mapping of a generalization violates a normal form, since many of its rows leave some columns NULL.



True

Older material sometimes says so, but NULLs alone do not break a normal form.



False

Right. Every column still depends on the key. The cost of the mapping is the NULLs themselves and what its foreign keys can no longer tell apart.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 6 Self-Checks
text:
Choosing and Naming Keys
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The customer table has the surrogate primary key customer_pk, and the designer leaves customer_number without a UNIQUE constraint, since the table already has a key. A clerk then enters customer C-1001 a second time. What happens?



The primary key refuses the second row

The primary key compares surrogate values, and the second row receives a new one.



The row is accepted: the table now holds two rows for C-1001, each with its own surrogate key

Yes. A surrogate key adds to the natural key; it does not replace it. Only the UNIQUE constraint on the business identifier stops the duplicate.



PostgreSQL merges the two rows

A database never merges rows on its own. It accepts a row or refuses it.



The insert is refused because customer_number is NOT NULL

NOT NULL requires a value; it does not compare one row’s value with another’s.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Blaha and Premerlani, whose method of mapping the book follows, call the two kinds of primary key value-based and existence-based identity. Which is a surrogate key?



Value-based identity

Value-based identity is a natural key, made of the class’s own attributes, such as a part’s number.



Existence-based identity

Yes. A surrogate key identifies a row because the row exists, not by any value the business records. PostgreSQL generates it, and it means nothing outside the database.



Neither; a surrogate key is not a primary key

The book’s database gives every table a surrogate primary key.



Both, depending on the column’s type

The kind of identity depends on where the key comes from, not on its type.



Check Show answer Reset



3. True or False: PostgreSQL checks a foreign key of two columns even when one of the two columns in the referring row is NULL.



True

PostgreSQL does not check a composite foreign key when any of its columns is NULL.



False

Right. A row with a NULL in one column of a composite foreign key passes the foreign key unchecked, so a design that relies on such a key declares its columns NOT NULL.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 6 Self-Checks
text:
Review of the Whole Chapter
Read the chapter summary

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Designing a database has two phases. This chapter’s mapping is the first, from a class model to a relational schema. What is the second?



Drawing the class model from the problem statement

The class model comes before the mapping; it is what the first phase starts from.



Turning the relational schema into statements that a database system runs to create the tables

Yes. The complete relational schema holds everything those statements need: columns, types, NULL rules, keys, checks, and deletion rules.



Normalizing the class model

Normal form is reviewed in step 7 of the mapping itself, on the tables.



Loading the tables with data

Data is loaded once the tables exist. Creating them is the second phase of the design.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Which of these rules do the tables leave to a checking query, so that the database accepts data that breaks them? Select every one.
Select all that apply.



With a table for each class, every part is in exactly one subclass table

Yes. Nothing stops a part from being in both subclass tables, or in neither.



The leads of operators form a hierarchy, with no loop

Yes. A CHECK refuses an operator as the operator’s own lead, but a longer loop satisfies both the foreign key and the CHECK.



Every order line has a quantity greater than zero

The CHECK on quantity refuses a quantity of zero or less.



Every order line refers to a product that exists

The foreign key product_fk refuses a line for a product that is not in product.



A part is not its own component

A CHECK that assembly_fk differs from component_fk refuses that.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Which of these constructs of a class model map to a table of their own, rather than to a foreign key in an existing table? Select every one.
Select all that apply.



A many-to-many association between warehouses and products

Yes. Neither end’s table can hold its links as one value, so the links become rows of a table of their own.



A ternary association among operators, machines, and work orders, with 0..* at every end

Yes. Each link connects three objects, so each row holds three foreign keys, which together are a key.



A one-to-many association between customers and their orders

Each order has one customer, so the link fits in the order’s row as a foreign key.



A qualified association between an order and its lines

Each line belongs to exactly one order, so the link fits in the line’s own row, as a foreign key.



A recursive one-to-many association from each operator to the operator’s lead

Each operator has at most one lead, so the link fits in the operator’s own row, as a foreign key to its own table.

title: Chapter 4 Self-Checks
section: The Shape of an Analytical Query and Grouping
text:
The Shape of an Analytical Query and Grouping
Read the sections

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. A query computes COUNT(*), SUM(quantity), MIN(unit_price), MAX(unit_price), and AVG(unit_price) over the 22 order lines of stage D5, with no GROUP BY. How many rows does it return?



22, one for each order line

An aggregate returns one value from many rows. The lines are summarized, not listed.



Five, one for each aggregate

The aggregates are columns of the result, not rows.



One

Yes. Without GROUP BY, every aggregate is computed over all the rows that the WHERE clause kept, and the result has exactly one row.



None; aggregates need a GROUP BY

An aggregate may summarize the whole table. GROUP BY is needed only to have one summary per group.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A query groups the order lines by product_fk, unit_price. What does each group hold?



Every line of one product

That would be GROUP BY product_fk. Adding unit_price divides each product’s lines further.



The lines of one product sold at one price, so a product sold at two prices forms two groups

Yes. A group is formed for each different combination of the grouping columns. That answers a different question from the units of each product.



Every line sold at one price, whatever the product

The groups are formed by both columns together, so two products at the same price stay apart.



One line each, since no two lines share both values

Several lines of a product often share a price, and they share a group.



Check Show answer Reset



3. Which aggregate gives each product’s total value ordered, the sum of quantity times unit price over its lines, when the lines are grouped by product?



SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price)

Yes. An aggregate may take any expression: the product is computed for each line, and then the values are summed.



SUM(l.quantity) * SUM(l.unit_price)

This multiplies the total units by the sum of every line’s price, which is no value at all.



SUM(l.quantity) * AVG(l.unit_price)

This matches the total only when every line of the product has the same price. A large line at a low price makes it wrong.



COUNT(*) * MAX(l.unit_price)

COUNT(*) counts lines, not units, and the highest price is not the price of every line.



Check Show answer Reset



4. A query counts orders by month with GROUP BY EXTRACT(MONTH FROM order_date), over the orders placed from January 2026 through March 2027. What goes wrong?



Nothing; each month is one group

EXTRACT(MONTH ...) gives only the month’s number, 1 to 12, whatever the year.



January, February, and March of 2026 fall into the same groups as those months of 2027

Yes. A group is formed for each different value of the grouping expression, and the month’s number alone does not tell the two years apart. Grouping by the year as well keeps them apart.



PostgreSQL refuses to group by an expression

A group may be formed by any expression, not only a column.



Each order becomes a group of its own

Orders placed in the same month share a value of the expression, and so share a group.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 4 Self-Checks
text:
Filtering Groups
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The counting method finds the operators certified on every Machining machine: it counts each operator’s certifications on Machining machines and keeps the operators whose count equals the number of Machining machines. What makes counting certifications the same as counting machines?



The alternate key (operator_fk, machine_fk) of certification allows at most one row for each operator and machine

Yes. Without that key, a repeated certification would be counted twice, and an operator certified twice on one machine would look certified on two.



COUNT(*) counts only the different machines in a group

COUNT(*) counts rows. It is the key that rules out a second row for the same operator and machine.



HAVING removes repeated rows within each group

HAVING keeps or discards whole groups. It removes nothing within one.



Each operator is certified on only one machine

An operator may hold many certifications. The key limits each operator to one for each machine.



Check Show answer Reset



2. In the same counting query, the condition m.work_center_fk = 2 in WHERE keeps only the certifications on Machining machines. Suppose it were left out, while HAVING still compares each count with the number of Machining machines, which is 2. What would go wrong?



Nothing, since HAVING already names the Machining work center

The subquery in HAVING counts Machining’s machines. It does not restrict which certifications each operator’s group counts.



Each count would include certifications on machines of other work centers, so an operator certified on one Machining machine and one welder would be kept

Yes. The rows must be restricted to the work center before they are grouped and counted, which is the job of WHERE.



Every operator would be kept

Only the operators with exactly two certifications in all would be kept, which is still the wrong list.



PostgreSQL would refuse the query

The query is valid. It answers a different question, with no message.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A planner wants the largest number of orders placed in any one month. Which approach gives it, and still shows every month if two months tie?



Rank the months by their counts with a window function, and keep rank 1 in the same query’s WHERE clause

A window function cannot be tested in WHERE, which is evaluated before it.



Group by month, then ORDER BY the count descending with LIMIT 1

This finds the busiest month, but a tie would show only one of the tied months.



A common table expression that counts the orders of each month, then a query that keeps the months whose count equals the largest count

Yes. The first step groups and the second summarizes the groups. Keeping every month equal to the maximum keeps all the tied months.



Group by month with HAVING COUNT(*) > 0

This keeps every month that had an order; it does not pick out the busiest.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 4 Self-Checks
text:
CASE Expressions
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Which value does this expression give an order line of 25 units?
CASE
  WHEN quantity >= 10 THEN 'large'
  WHEN quantity >= 20 THEN 'very large'
  ELSE 'small'
END



'large'

Yes. The conditions are tested in order, and the value of the first true one is returned. Since every line of 20 units or more also has 10 or more, 'very large' can never be returned; the larger threshold must be tested first.



'very large'

The second condition is true, but the first already was, and CASE stops at the first true condition.



Both values, one after the other

A CASE expression returns one value for each row.



'small'

ELSE is reached only when no condition is true.



Check Show answer Reset



2. When may a CASE expression be written in the shorter form CASE unit_of_measure WHEN 'EA' THEN 'each' WHEN 'FT' THEN 'feet' ELSE 'unknown' END?



When every condition compares one expression with a value

Yes. The shorter form names the expression once, after CASE, and each WHEN gives a value to match.



Only when the expression has no ELSE

The shorter form may have an ELSE, as this one does.



Whenever the conditions test ranges, such as quantity >= 10

A range is not a match with one value. Such conditions need the full form, with a condition in each WHEN.



Only in the SELECT list

A CASE expression of either form may stand anywhere a value may.



Check Show answer Reset



3. The production manager’s morning list sorts the work orders with ORDER BY CASE WHEN completed_on IS NULL THEN 1 WHEN completed_on > due_on THEN 2 ELSE 3 END, due_on, work_order_number. Which statement about it is true?



The CASE must also appear in the SELECT list

A CASE expression may stand anywhere a value may. Here it is used only to sort.



The CASE gives each work order a rank that appears in no column of the result, and the rows are sorted by that rank first and by due date within it

Yes. The open work orders lead, then the late ones, then the rest. A sort like this replaces a report’s hand-arranged sections.



The rows are sorted by due date first, and the CASE breaks ties

The expressions sort in the order they are named, so the rank comes first.



The query must group by the CASE expression to use it in ORDER BY

Nothing is grouped. The expression is computed for each row and used as a sort key.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 4 Self-Checks
text:
Window Functions
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Suppose four customers placed 45, 45, 40, and 38 orders. A query ranks them with RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) and with DENSE_RANK() over the same order. What ranks does each give the customer with 40 orders?



3 from both

DENSE_RANK skips nothing after a tie.



2 from both

RANK skips the ranks that tied rows use up.



3 from RANK and 2 from DENSE_RANK

Yes. Both give the two tied customers rank 1. RANK then gives 3, since two customers finished ahead, and DENSE_RANK gives the next rank, 2.



2 from RANK and 3 from DENSE_RANK

This reverses the two functions.



Check Show answer Reset



2. Suppose a product has four order lines: 10 units ordered on January 5, 5 units and 15 units both ordered on January 9, and 20 units ordered on January 12. What does SUM(quantity) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) show on the line of 5 units?



15, the 10 units before it and its own 5

That counts the rows one at a time. The default frame also takes in the current row’s peers, the rows that tie with it on the ORDER BY columns.



30

Yes. With an ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the frame runs from the first row to the current row and its peers. Both January 9 lines are in it, so both show 10 + 5 + 15 = 30.



50, the total of all four lines

The frame ends at the current row’s last peer, not at the end of the partition.



5, the line’s own quantity

The frame begins at the partition’s first row, so the running total includes January 5.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A five-inspection moving average uses ROWS BETWEEN 4 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, ordered by inspection time. The axle diameter was inspected once on each weekday from June 8 to 16, 2026, and not on June 13 and 14, a weekend. Which inspections are in the frame of June 16?



June 12, 15, and 16, the inspections of the last five days

ROWS counts rows, not days. The weekend holds no rows, so the frame reaches further back.



June 10, 11, 12, 15, and 16

Yes. The frame holds the current row and the four rows before it, whatever their dates.



All seven inspections from June 8 to 16

The frame holds five rows at most: the current row and the four before it.



June 11, 12, 15, and 16

4 PRECEDING adds four rows to the current row, so the frame holds five.



Check Show answer Reset



4. Which of these requests need two steps, a common table expression that computes the window function and a query that reads it? Select every one that does.
Select all that apply.



The customers whose dense rank by number of orders is at most 3

Yes. A window function cannot appear in WHERE or HAVING, since both are evaluated before it, so the filter on its result is a second step.



The order lines whose unit price is below the average price of their product

Yes. The product’s average comes from a window function, and the condition that compares each line with it cannot be written in WHERE, so it is a second step.



Each order line beside the average price of its product

One query does this, with AVG(unit_price) OVER (PARTITION BY product_fk).



Each inspection beside the measurement of the inspection before it, over all the inspections

LAG in a single query does this, since nothing is filtered on its result.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 4 Self-Checks
text:
Recursive Queries
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Suppose a data-entry error records part A as a component of part B, and part B as a component of part A. What happens when a bill of materials explosion reaches them?



The database notices the repeated part and stops with an error

Nothing in a plain recursive query compares a new row with earlier ones; with UNION ALL a part found again is simply added again.



The explosion lists A and B once each and continues

Each step finds the other part again, so the two never stop producing rows.



Every step produces another row, so the query never ends unless it bounds the depth or detects the cycle

Yes. A recursive query stops only when a step produces no rows. A condition such as WHERE e.depth < 20 in the recursive part, or the CYCLE clause of PostgreSQL 14 and later, ends it.



The anchor finds no rows, so the result is empty

The anchor finds the starting product as usual; the trouble begins in the steps below it.



Check Show answer Reset



2. True or False: in each run of the recursive part, the database joins every row found so far to bom_line.



True

If it did, a part found in an earlier step would be exploded again in every later step, and its components would be repeated.



False

Correct. Each run sees only the working table, the rows the previous step produced. A part found in step 1 is exploded in step 2 and not again.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A bill of materials uses the same hardware kit in two places in one product’s structure. Which choice between UNION and UNION ALL in the recursive query is right for a quantity explosion, and why?



UNION, since a part should appear only once in a list of materials

UNION removes rows that repeat exactly, so when both places give the same row the second is lost, and the kit’s quantity is understated.



UNION ALL, since the kit must appear once for each place it is used

Yes. Each place contributes its own quantity, and keeping every row keeps them all. UNION suits a list of distinct parts, not quantities.



Either, since the two give the same rows when the quantities differ

They happen to agree only when no row repeats exactly; an explosion should not depend on that.



Neither; a recursive query needs a join in place of a union

A recursive common table expression is an anchor and a recursive part joined by a union.



Check Show answer Reset



4. Suppose one product uses 3 of an assembly, each assembly uses 4 of a component, and each component is cut from 0.5 feet of bar stock. How many feet of bar stock does the explosion report for one product?



0.5

That is the bar stock in one component. The quantities multiply down the chain.



7.5

This adds the quantities. Each level multiplies its parent’s quantity by the component’s quantity_per.



6

Yes. 3 assemblies times 4 components each is 12 components, and 12 times 0.5 feet is 6 feet.



12

That is the number of components; each needs only half a foot of bar stock.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 4 Self-Checks
text:
Analytical Queries on Operational Data
Read the section

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. The days-of-supply query divides each stock level’s quantity on hand, from the stock_level table, by a daily rate computed from a year of shipments. The year of history in stage G does not update stock_level. What does the result therefore measure?



How long each warehouse’s stock lasted on each day of the year

The stock levels hold one recorded quantity each. Nothing in them changes from day to day.



The recorded stock against a year’s demand, not a real warehouse’s stock tracked day by day

Yes. The comparison is still useful for ranking urgency, but its stock figures are the ones on record, not the result of the year’s shipments.



The stock left after the year’s shipments are subtracted

The query subtracts nothing. It divides the recorded quantity by the daily rate.



The average stock held over the year

The query reads one quantity per stock level, not a history of quantities.



Check Show answer Reset



2. An individuals chart’s limits are computed from the average moving range, the absolute difference between consecutive measurements, found with LAG. Which statements about that query are true? Select every one that is.
Select all that apply.



The moving ranges are computed in a common table expression, and the aggregates read its result

Yes. LAG is a window function, computed after any grouping, so the averages of its results come in a second step.



The constant 2.66 converts the average moving range into three standard deviations of the process

Yes. The limits are the center line, the average measurement, plus and minus 2.66 times the average moving range.



The moving range must be computed in HAVING, after the measurements are grouped

LAG is a window function, which cannot appear in HAVING, and nothing here is grouped.



A measurement outside the limits proves that the process is out of specification

Control limits come from the process’s own variation, not from the specification. A point outside them signals a cause worth investigating.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A days-of-supply query divides a year’s units shipped by 365 to get each product’s daily rate. For a product first sold in September of that year, what does that do to its days of supply?



Nothing, since the year’s total includes every unit shipped

The total is right, but it is spread over months in which the product was not for sale.



It understates the daily rate, so the days of supply looks longer and the product less urgent than it is

Yes. The units were sold over about seven months, not twelve, so the true daily rate is higher.



It overstates the daily rate, so the product looks more urgent than it is

Dividing by more days than the product was sold makes the rate smaller, not larger.



The query returns NULL for that product

The product has shipments, so its sum and rate are numbers, just misleading ones.



Check Show answer Reset

title: Chapter 4 Self-Checks
text:
Review of the Whole Chapter
Read the chapter summary

Self-CheckClear all answers


1. Which of these requests need a window function, rather than GROUP BY alone? Select every one that does.
Select all that apply.



Each order line beside the average price of its product

Yes. GROUP BY keeps one row per product; a window function keeps every line and adds its group’s average.



A running total of units ordered, date by date

Yes. SUM with an ORDER BY inside OVER gives each row the total of its frame.



Each inspection’s change from the inspection before it

Yes. LAG reaches into the previous row of the order.



The total units ordered of each product

One row per product is exactly what GROUP BY returns.



The number of orders placed in each month

One row per month is exactly what GROUP BY returns.



Check Show answer Reset



2. A query has a WHERE clause, a GROUP BY, a HAVING clause, and a window function in its SELECT list. Which statement about it is true?



HAVING may test the window function’s result

HAVING is evaluated before the window function, and PostgreSQL refuses a window function there.



The window function may order the groups by an aggregate, since the groups and their aggregates exist before it is computed

Yes. This is how a query ranks customers by their number of orders in one step.



The window function is computed before GROUP BY, so it sees the table’s rows rather than the groups

Window functions are computed after GROUP BY, HAVING, and the SELECT list, over one row for each group.



DISTINCT removes repeated rows before the window function is computed

DISTINCT comes after the window functions in the order of evaluation.



Check Show answer Reset



3. A quality engineer asks for the median completion time of the completed work orders for each manufactured part. Which parts does the query need? Select every one it does.
Select all that apply.



GROUP BY the manufactured part

Yes. “For each manufactured part” names the groups.



PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY ...) on the completion time

Yes. The median is the 0.5 percentile, and the values it orders are named after WITHIN GROUP.



A window function with OVER

The request wants one row per manufactured part, not every work order beside its group’s median.



WITH RECURSIVE

Nothing in the request follows a chain of rows.



An ORDER BY on the completion time at the end of the query

The order a percentile needs is given inside the aggregate, after WITHIN GROUP. Sorting the result computes nothing.



Check Show answer Reset
